items.title: Elephants need hairs to STAY COOL
items.claim: Big animals are well-insulated by sheer size — surface area to volume ratio drops as you scale up. So why do elephants have sparse but persistent hairs, in a hot environment where insulation is the last thing they need?
items.prompt: What's the function of an elephant's hairs?

options.text: Insulation against the cold
They INCREASE convective heat loss — the sparse hairs disrupt the still air layer at the skin surface and allow more efficient cooling than bare skin would
Camouflage
Vestigial — they have no function

items.reveal_title: Surface area scaling and thermal management
items.reveal:
Animal mass scales as length cubed; surface area as length squared. Doubling an animal's linear size doubles its surface-to-volume ratio's inverse — large animals have proportionally less surface area to dump heat through.

Elephants generate huge metabolic heat (about 2500 watts at rest for a 4 tonne adult) but have proportionally tiny skin. They are constantly battling overheating. Their hairs, ears (huge for their body), wallowing in mud, and behavioural cooling all serve heat dissipation.

Cordeschi and colleagues (2012) modelled elephant hair density and showed sparse hairs improve heat loss by about 5 to 20 percent — likely a real evolutionary purpose.
items.why: Hair is associated with warmth. For animals at the wrong end of the surface-to-volume scaling, hair can do the opposite.

items.title: Cells make energy by pumping ACID uphill
items.claim: Mitochondria spend most of their energy budget pumping protons across the inner membrane against a steep electrochemical gradient. Only after building this acidic outer space do they let the protons flow back through ATP synthase, capturing the energy.
items.prompt: Why not just make ATP directly during electron transport?

options.text: Direct synthesis is technically impossible

Chemiosmosis lets the cell decouple ENERGY EXTRACTION (electron transport) from ENERGY USE (ATP synthesis); the proton gradient is a rechargeable battery that links any electron donor to any ATP demand
Mitochondria evolved before ATP existed
The gradient is a side-effect with no function

items.reveal_title: Mitchell's chemiosmotic hypothesis — initially dismissed, then Nobel-winning
items.reveal:
Peter Mitchell proposed in 1961 that ATP synthesis was driven by a proton gradient, not by direct chemistry. Biochemists hated the idea — it seemed to require a 'metabolic battery' instead of a chemical intermediate. Mitchell was right, and won the 1978 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

The inner mitochondrial membrane is impermeable to protons. Electrons flowing through the respiratory chain pump protons OUT, building a pH gradient (~ 0.7 units) and an electric potential (~ 150 mV) — together about 200 mV of proton motive force.

ATP synthase is essentially a rotary motor turned by proton flow. The number of protons per ATP is fractional (about 3.7 to 4) because synthase geometry doesn't match the chemistry of ATP cleanly.
items.why: Energy currency feels like chemistry. Living cells use a physical gradient — a battery — as the actual unit of energy transfer.

items.title: Bacteria swap genes like trading cards
items.claim: Sexual reproduction is supposedly biology's great innovation for mixing genes. Bacteria don't bother. They share DNA fragments — including whole antibiotic-resistance genes — directly between unrelated species, sometimes across genera.
items.prompt: What's the consequence for evolution?

options.text: Bacteria can't really evolve
Useful mutations spread across the bacterial 'pan-genome' far faster than vertical inheritance allows — antibiotic resistance can jump from one species to another in a single transfer event
Bacteria only share genes within the same species
Horizontal transfer is too rare to matter

items.reveal_title: Three mechanisms keep the bacterial gene pool fluid
items.reveal:
Conjugation: two bacteria form a physical bridge (pilus) and transfer a plasmid.
Transformation: bacteria scoop up loose DNA from the environment.
Transduction: viruses (phages) accidentally package bacterial DNA and inject it into the next host.

The NDM-1 resistance gene, first found in Klebsiella in 2008, jumped via plasmids across at least 11 bacterial species and 4 continents within a decade. Genes encoding beta-lactamases (penicillin breakdown) appear in soil bacteria; clinical pathogens picked them up after antibiotics entered hospitals.

The 'tree of life' for bacteria isn't really a tree — it's a tangled net.
items.why: Evolution is taught as descent with modification along branching lineages. Bacterial evolution is reticular — sideways, not just downward.

items.title: A woman who died in 1951 still has dividing cells today
items.claim: Normal human cells divide about 50 times and then stop (the Hayflick limit). HeLa cells, taken from Henrietta Lacks's cervical tumour in 1951, divide indefinitely. They are in laboratories on every continent.
items.prompt: What makes HeLa cells 'immortal'?

options.text: They are not human cells

Constitutive expression of telomerase — the enzyme that rebuilds telomeres on chromosome ends — allows them to divide without losing telomeric DNA, bypassing the Hayflick limit. The HPV-derived oncogenes E6 and E7 also disable normal tumour suppressors
Special preservation chemicals keep them alive
All cancer cells are technically immortal

items.reveal_title: Telomeres, telomerase, and the loophole around cell senescence
items.reveal:
Linear chromosomes lose a small amount of DNA from their ends with each replication (the 'end replication problem'). Once telomeres reach a critical short length, cells trigger senescence — the Hayflick limit, named after Leonard Hayflick (1961).

Most adult cells suppress telomerase. Germline cells, stem cells and most cancers reactivate it. HeLa cells express telomerase robustly. Combined with disabled tumour suppressors (p53 and Rb, neutralised by HPV-18 oncoproteins), they grow without limit.

HeLa cells were the first immortal human cell line. They were taken without Henrietta Lacks's consent. The ethical legacy is still being addressed — her family didn't learn the cells existed until 1973, and only signed an agreement with the NIH on access to her genome in 2013.
items.why: Cell death is taught as inevitable. The cellular machinery to bypass it exists; cancer cells exploit it; HeLa cells made it visible.

items.title: Eyes have evolved independently more than 40 times
items.claim: Eyes are complicated. Darwin worried about them in Origin of Species. Modern phylogenetics shows that eyes — from basic photoreceptors to full image-forming structures — have evolved independently somewhere between 40 and 60 times across animal lineages.
items.prompt: What does this tell us about evolution?

options.text: Eyes are too complex to evolve once, let alone many times

Photoreception is selected for so strongly that wherever a workable starting point exists (a light-sensitive protein) selection assembles eyes; complex outcomes evolve repeatedly when the gradient of advantage is steep
All eyes descend from a single ancestor
Vision is impossible without divine design

items.reveal_title: Eyes as evolutionary stress-tests for gradualism
items.reveal:
Modern eyes include: vertebrate camera eyes, cephalopod camera eyes (independently evolved, no blind spot), trilobite calcite-lens compound eyes, scallop mirror eyes, copepod parabolic-reflector eyes, jumping-spider sharp-focus eyes, brittle-star whole-body lensed skin.

Nilsson and Pelger (1994) modelled the evolution of a vertebrate-style camera eye from a flat patch of photoreceptors. With realistic mutation rates and selection coefficients of 1 percent, they estimated 400,000 generations — about half a million years — to produce a fully functional eye.

The common element across all 40+ origins: opsin proteins. The receptor molecules are conserved; the architectures around them have been built and rebuilt many times.
items.why: Eyes feel like such complex organs that they 'must' be hard to evolve. They are exactly the kind of thing selection invents many times when given a good starting molecule.

items.title: Octopuses change colour while being colour-blind
items.claim: Cephalopods produce sophisticated colour displays — mimicking corals, fish, sand — using chromatophore cells embedded in the skin. Their actual eyes have only one photoreceptor type. They cannot distinguish red from green.
items.prompt: How do octopuses match colour without seeing it?

options.text: They have hidden colour vision we haven't found
Their SKIN contains opsin proteins — the same light-sensitive receptors used in eyes — likely giving the surface itself wavelength-sensitivity that the eyes lack
They guess based on context
Other octopuses signal the colour to them

items.reveal_title: Distributed colour vision via opsin-expressing skin
items.reveal:
Cephalopod skin expresses several genes (including r-opsin and rhodopsin-like proteins) usually found in eyes. Ramirez and Oakley (2015) showed Octopus bimaculoides skin responds to specific wavelengths.

The hypothesis: the chromatic information bypasses the brain entirely. The skin senses ambient colour and adjusts the chromatophore display locally without needing centralised colour vision.

It's also possible they exploit the chromatic aberration of their unusual U-shaped pupils to extract colour information from a single photoreceptor type — Stubbs and Stubbs (2016) — but the experimental support is mixed. Either way, cephalopod colour matching is a fascinating biological riddle.
items.why: Vision is assumed to happen in eyes and brains. In cephalopods it may happen distributed across the body.

items.title: Water bears can survive being heated, frozen, irradiated and put in space
items.claim: Tardigrades dry out into a 'tun' state and become metabolically inert. In this state they survive temperatures from near absolute zero to over 150 degrees Celsius, 1000 times the lethal radiation dose for humans, and the vacuum of space.
items.prompt: How do they survive complete desiccation?

options.text: Special antifreeze proteins
Replacement of intracellular water with bioglasses (trehalose sugars and intrinsically disordered proteins like CAHS) that stabilise membranes and proteins in a vitrified state
Their cells contain no water in any state
Heat-shock proteins do everything

items.reveal:
In favourable conditions, tardigrades are ordinary aquatic micro-animals with ~1000 cells. When their environment dries, they curl into a tun and lose 97 to 99 percent of their water.

They replace it with trehalose (a disaccharide that vitrifies on drying, forming a glass that holds membranes and proteins in place) and tardigrade-specific intrinsically disordered proteins ('CAHS' — Cytoplasmic Abundant Heat Soluble) that gel into supporting matrices.

In the tun state, metabolism stops. Without water, biochemistry can't proceed — so most chemistry that would kill the tardigrade (radiation damage requires water-radical chemistry; freezing requires ice crystal formation) is paused.

Rehydrated tardigrades resume normal life within hours. The 2007 ESA FOTON-M3 mission exposed them to open space; many survived.
items.why: Life is associated with metabolism. Some animals turn metabolism off, dehydrate to a glass-like state, and re-start later — life as a paused process.

items.title: Information can flow from RNA back to DNA
items.claim: Crick's central dogma: DNA makes RNA makes protein. The arrow goes one way: DNA to RNA. But retroviruses — including HIV — carry an enzyme that copies their RNA genome back into DNA.
items.prompt: What does reverse transcription mean for the dogma?

options.text: The central dogma is wrong and discredited

Crick's original statement was about residue-level sequence transfer; reverse transcription does flow RNA-to-DNA, but the forbidden flow (protein-to-DNA) has never been observed — the dogma is more nuanced than the textbook version
Retroviruses are not really alive
Reverse transcription is a lab artefact

items.reveal_title: Crick's original dogma was more sophisticated than the cartoon
items.reveal:
Crick (1958) explicitly listed which residue-level transfers were possible (DNA to DNA, DNA to RNA, RNA to protein) and which were special transfers (RNA to RNA, RNA to DNA) — possible but not normally done. He also listed forbidden transfers (anything starting from protein).

Reverse transcriptase, discovered by Temin and Baltimore in 1970 (1975 Nobel), is the canonical 'special transfer'. HIV uses it to integrate into the host genome. Some retrotransposons in our own genomes do it constantly.

The forbidden transfers (protein to DNA, protein to RNA, protein to protein) remain forbidden. The dogma, taken literally as Crick wrote it, still stands.
items.why: Pop science presents 'the central dogma' as a rigid one-way arrow. The real dogma is a constraint on which directions sequence information can flow in, and reverse transcription was always allowed.

items.title: Bees die when they sting — and this makes evolutionary sense
items.claim: A worker bee that stings a mammal disembowels itself and dies. Sterile, suicidal workers shouldn't exist if natural selection works at the individual level. They do exist, abundantly.
items.prompt: How does evolution favour individuals that don't reproduce?

options.text: Natural selection doesn't really work for social insects

Hamilton's rule: a gene for altruism spreads if rB is greater than C (relatedness times benefit exceeds cost); worker bees share 75 percent of their genes with sisters due to haplodiploidy, so helping the queen reproduce passes on their own genes effectively
Queen bees control workers chemically against their interests
Workers will eventually reproduce

items.reveal:
W. D. Hamilton wrote the equation rB greater than C: a gene for helping behaviour spreads if the relatedness (r) times the benefit to the recipient (B) exceeds the cost to the actor (C).

In haplodiploid Hymenoptera (bees, ants, wasps), females are diploid (from a diploid mother and a haploid father), males are haploid (unfertilised eggs). A worker shares 50 percent of her genes with her own offspring (if she had any), but 75 percent with her full sisters — because their shared father is haploid and gave them ALL his genes.

So a worker's gene-propagation interest is best served by helping her mother (the queen) make more sisters. Sterility is rational from the gene's perspective.

Hamilton's work, building on J. B. S. Haldane's quip 'I would lay down my life for two brothers or eight cousins', founded sociobiology.
items.why: Selection is taught as acting on individuals. The gene's-eye view explains altruism, sociality and self-sacrifice — phenomena that the individual-level view can't easily handle.

items.title: Only 1.5 percent of human DNA codes for proteins
items.claim: The human genome has about 3 billion base pairs. Of these, only about 1.5 percent — 45 million bases — encode proteins. The rest was once called 'junk DNA'. Most of it isn't.
items.prompt: What does the non-coding majority actually do?

options.text: It's all junk left over from evolution

It includes promoters, enhancers, insulators, microRNA genes, long non-coding RNAs, ribosomal RNA, structural sequences, transposable elements (some still active), and regions whose function is still being mapped
It codes for proteins we haven't found
It's only present in cells that have stopped dividing

items.reveal_title: ENCODE and the redefinition of junk
items.reveal:
The ENCODE Project (2012) reported biochemical activity (transcription, transcription-factor binding, chromatin features) in about 80 percent of the genome. Whether all of this counts as 'function' was hotly debated.

Certain categories of non-coding DNA have clear roles:
- Promoters/enhancers: regulate gene expression in time and place. Disrupting them causes disease (e.g., enhancer mutations causing limb deformity).
- microRNAs: ~22-nucleotide RNAs that tune protein levels.
- Long non-coding RNAs: XIST silences a whole X chromosome in females.
- Transposable elements: about 45 percent of the genome; some still mobile.

Much DNA may also be 'spacer' or accumulated parasitic sequence with no current function — but the cell is full of layers of regulation built from non-coding DNA.
items.why: Genome size was thought to scale with organism complexity. Onions have 5 times more DNA than humans. Most DNA isn't there to encode proteins — and may be doing many things at once.

items.title: You are outnumbered by your own bacteria
items.claim: Adult humans carry about 38 trillion bacterial cells, roughly matching the count of human cells. By gene count, microbial DNA dwarfs human DNA by 100 to 1. They digest your food, train your immune system and affect your behaviour.
items.prompt: Which is more accurate?

options.text: Humans have 10 times more bacteria than human cells
The ratio is closer to 1.3:1 (bacteria:human), based on revised counts (Sender, Fuchs & Milo 2016) — much closer than the older 10:1 figure suggested
There are about as many bacterial cells as human red blood cells
Bacterial cell count is roughly the same as human muscle cell count

items.reveal:
The famous 10:1 ratio came from a 1972 back-of-envelope estimate by Thomas Luckey. It propagated through textbooks for 40 years.

In 2016, Sender, Fuchs and Milo revisited the numbers. They estimated about 30 trillion human cells (84 percent red blood cells) and 38 trillion bacterial cells (most in the colon). The ratio is close to 1:1.

Gene count is a different story. Each human cell carries 20,000 genes; the gut microbiome contains an estimated 2 to 20 million unique microbial genes — so by gene count, we're 99 percent microbe.

The gut microbiome makes vitamins, ferments fibre, modulates the immune system and produces neurotransmitters that may affect mood and behaviour (the 'gut-brain axis').
items.why: Self/other has clear boundaries in popular imagination. Biologically, the boundary is fuzzy and statistical.

items.title: Your mitochondria used to be a separate organism
items.claim: Mitochondria have their own DNA, their own ribosomes, a double membrane, and divide independently of the cell. About 2 billion years ago, a free-living alpha-proteobacterium got engulfed by another cell and stayed.
items.prompt: What's the strongest evidence mitochondria were once independent?

options.text: They are smaller than the host cell

Mitochondrial DNA is circular (like a bacterial chromosome), their ribosomes resemble bacterial ribosomes (and are inhibited by antibiotics like chloramphenicol), and their inner membrane has bacteria-like lipid composition
They contain DNA
They use ATP

items.reveal_title: Lynn Margulis and the endosymbiotic theory
items.reveal:
Lynn Margulis proposed in 1967 that mitochondria descend from free-living alpha-proteobacteria, and chloroplasts from cyanobacteria. Her paper was rejected fifteen times before being accepted. The orthodoxy disliked the idea of major evolution happening by merger rather than gradual modification.

The evidence accumulated:
- Circular DNA in mitochondria and chloroplasts.
- Bacterial-style ribosomes; sensitive to bacterial antibiotics.
- Double membranes (the outer from the host cell, the inner from the bacterium).
- Replication by binary fission, independent of cell division.
- Phylogenetic analysis: mitochondrial genes group with Rickettsia (intracellular alpha-proteobacteria).

All eukaryotes (including animals, plants, fungi) descend from this single ancient merger. Without it, complex life wouldn't exist.
items.why: Evolution is taught as branching divergence. Some of the most important steps came from merger — two organisms becoming one.

items.title: Each of your sperm/eggs is one of 2 to the 23rd power possibilities
items.claim: Meiosis shuffles 23 chromosome pairs into 23 gametes. From you alone, ignoring recombination, that's 8.4 million possible combinations. Add crossing over and the count is effectively infinite. Why is sexual reproduction so expensive to maintain?
items.prompt: Why has sex (rather than cloning) persisted in almost all eukaryotes?

options.text: Sex is uniformly better than cloning

Sex generates genetic variation that helps populations adapt to changing environments (the Red Queen hypothesis: ongoing host-parasite arms races favour variability); also recombination weeds out accumulated harmful mutations more efficiently than clonal lineages can
It's just historical inertia
Sex is necessary for cell division

items.reveal_title: The twofold cost and the Red Queen
items.reveal:
A sexually reproducing female passes 50 percent of her genes to each offspring. An asexual female passes 100 percent. Asexual lineages should outcompete sexual ones by a factor of two each generation. They mostly don't.

Leading explanations:
- Red Queen (Hamilton, Van Valen): parasites and pathogens evolve to attack common host genotypes; sexual reproduction keeps host genotypes shifting so parasites can't catch up.
- Muller's ratchet: asexual lineages accumulate harmful mutations and cannot purge them efficiently. Recombination lets harmful mutations be separated from beneficial ones.
- Fisher-Muller: sex can combine beneficial mutations from different lineages.

Observationally, almost all asexual lineages are evolutionarily young, suggesting they accumulate problems and go extinct.
items.why: Sex's costs are enormous and obvious; its benefits are subtle and long-term. Evolution favours it anyway, and the reasons are still debated.

items.title: Enzymes don't 'fit' substrates — they fit transition states
items.claim: The textbook 'lock and key' model says enzymes have an active site that matches the substrate. Real enzymes are much more interesting: they bind the TRANSITION STATE of the reaction more tightly than the substrate or product.
items.prompt: Why does binding the transition state make a better catalyst?

options.text: It doesn't matter what the enzyme binds tightly
Stabilising the highest-energy point in the reaction lowers the activation energy; an enzyme that binds the transition state by 1000-fold relative to substrate accelerates the reaction by 1000-fold
Binding the substrate tightly always speeds up reactions
The substrate spontaneously becomes the transition state

items.reveal_title: Linus Pauling's prediction and modern enzyme design
items.reveal:
Pauling proposed in 1948 that enzymes catalyse reactions by binding most strongly to the transition state, lowering the activation energy.

Direct evidence: 'transition state analogues' — stable molecules that mimic the transition state's geometry — bind enzymes 10 to 10,000 times more tightly than the substrates themselves. Many drugs are designed this way (statins like atorvastatin mimic the transition state of HMG-CoA reductase).

Catalytic antibodies, raised against transition state analogues, can catalyse reactions for which no natural enzyme exists (Schultz, Lerner, 1986). De novo enzyme design (Baker lab, 2008 onward) explicitly engineers active sites to fit predicted transition states.

The induced-fit model (Koshland 1958) and the transition-state model are both refinements of the original lock-and-key.
items.why: Lock-and-key implies stable binding of stable molecules. Enzymes catalyse by binding unstable, fleeting transition states — a much subtler picture.

items.title: Your liver and your eyes have separate clocks
items.claim: Every cell in your body has its own molecular clock. The 'master' clock in the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) synchronises them. Eating at the wrong time can desynchronise organs from each other — same as jet lag without the travel.
items.prompt: What is a cellular circadian clock made of?

options.text: A specialised time-sensing organelle

A transcription-translation feedback loop: genes (BMAL1/CLOCK in mammals) drive expression of inhibitor proteins (PER, CRY) that themselves repress the original genes — the cycle takes about 24 hours to complete
An internal sundial of pigment molecules
Hormones from the pituitary

items.reveal:
In Drosophila, Hall, Rosbash and Young identified Period (PER) gene and worked out the negative feedback loop: PER protein accumulates in the cell, eventually shuts down its own transcription, then degrades, allowing the cycle to repeat. Mammals have BMAL1/CLOCK driving PER1/2/3 and CRY1/2, with the same logic.

The cycle's intrinsic period is close to 24 hours; light input (via melanopsin in retinal ganglion cells) synchronises it to the day.

Peripheral clocks (in liver, muscle, fat) entrain primarily to feeding times. Eating at midnight tells your liver it's daytime even as your SCN says it's night — exactly the desynchronisation seen in shift workers, who have elevated rates of metabolic disease and some cancers.
items.why: The biological clock is pictured as one master organ. Every cell has one, and keeping them aligned is a daily ongoing process — and easily disrupted.

items.title: Your body can make antibodies against molecules that don't exist yet
items.claim: Humans have about 20,000 genes. We make perhaps 10 to the 11 different antibody molecules — far more than our genome could encode directly. Including antibodies against viruses we'll never meet.
items.prompt: How do we generate such enormous antibody diversity?

options.text: Each antibody is encoded by a separate gene

V(D)J recombination — during B cell development, gene segments (V, D, J) are randomly chosen and joined with imprecise cuts, and then somatic hypermutation refines the result during an immune response
Antibodies are made up new for each encounter from scratch
The genome reshuffles itself constantly in all cells

items.reveal_title: Tonegawa's discovery — recombination in somatic cells
items.reveal:
Susumu Tonegawa (Nobel 1987) showed that B cells deliberately rearrange their immunoglobulin genes. Each B cell randomly picks one V, one D and one J segment for the heavy chain (V and J for the light chain), joins them with imprecise junctions (adding/deleting nucleotides), and pairs heavy with light. The combinatorial maths gives about 10 to the 11 possible specificities from a few hundred gene segments.

Once a B cell encounters its antigen, somatic hypermutation introduces additional point mutations into the variable region, and selection retains the best binders (affinity maturation).

The result is an immune system that can respond to virtually any molecular shape — including ones never seen before, like artificial drugs.
items.why: Genome size limits direct encoding. The immune system uses combinatorics and somatic mutation to overshoot what the genome alone could specify.

items.title: Neurons don't 'fire harder' — they fire faster or not at all
items.claim: A neuron's action potential is all-or-nothing. The size of every action potential in a given neuron is essentially identical. Strong stimuli don't make bigger spikes — they make more spikes per second.
items.prompt: How is signal intensity encoded?

options.text: By the amplitude of each action potential
By the FREQUENCY of action potentials (and by the pattern of which neurons fire and when) — the rate code is the simplest model, but timing and synchrony also carry information
By the colour of the signal
By the chemical identity of each spike

items.reveal_title: Edgar Adrian and the discovery of the rate code
items.reveal:
Edgar Adrian (Nobel 1932) recorded from single sensory neurons in frogs and found: stretch a muscle and the neuron fires more spikes per second. Spike amplitude didn't change. The signal was the frequency.

Action potentials are regenerative — voltage-gated sodium channels self-amplify any membrane depolarisation past threshold into a stereotyped spike, then sodium channels inactivate and potassium channels repolarise. Sub-threshold stimuli produce no spike at all; supra-threshold stimuli produce one spike, of fixed size.

The brain reads intensity from spike rate, fine timing from spike intervals, and 'identity' from which neurons fired. Some neural systems (auditory, visual) encode information in spike timing to within a millisecond.
items.why: Sensory intensity feels continuous. The neuron encoding it is digital — and the continuous sensation is reconstructed from spike statistics.

items.title: The most abundant enzyme on Earth is bad at its job
items.claim: Rubisco fixes carbon dioxide into sugar in every photosynthesising organism. It's the most abundant protein on the planet (about half a kilogram in every square metre of leaf). It's also slow (3 reactions per second per active site) and confuses CO2 with O2.
items.prompt: Why do plants invest so heavily in such a flawed enzyme?

options.text: There's no alternative — Rubisco is the only carbon-fixation enzyme that works

Rubisco evolved when the atmosphere had little O2; the confusion between CO2 and O2 was rare then. Now plants mass-produce it (often 50 percent of leaf protein) to compensate for its slowness, and C4 plants concentrate CO2 around it to outcompete O2 binding
Other enzymes break Rubisco quickly
Rubisco is highly efficient — the textbook is wrong

items.reveal:
Rubisco's active site binds CO2 by inserting it into a bound substrate (ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate). About 25 percent of the time at room temperature, it grabs O2 instead — initiating photorespiration, a wasteful cycle that costs energy and releases CO2.

This was tolerable in the Proterozoic atmosphere (low O2, high CO2). As oxygen rose and CO2 dropped, the problem grew.

C4 plants (corn, sugarcane) evolved an extra carbon-fixation step in mesophyll cells (using PEP carboxylase, which doesn't confuse O2). This shuttles CO2 into specialised bundle-sheath cells at high concentration, where Rubisco then operates without interference.

CAM plants (cacti, pineapples) do the same trick temporally — fixing CO2 at night when stomata can be open without losing water.
items.why: Evolution doesn't engineer optimal enzymes — it tinkers around constraints inherited from earlier conditions. Rubisco is a beautiful example of a molecular legacy system.

items.title: Famine in 1944 affected the grandchildren of survivors
items.claim: The Dutch Hongerwinter (1944-1945) caused severe famine for several months. Decades later, the GRANDchildren of women pregnant during the famine showed altered methylation patterns and different rates of metabolic disease — even though they were never themselves underfed.
items.prompt: How does an environmental stress affect three generations?

options.text: Coincidence — the effect isn't real

Epigenetic marks (especially DNA methylation patterns) acquired during fetal development can persist into adulthood; some can affect germline cells, allowing the next generation to inherit the modified pattern
It must be a DNA sequence mutation caused by famine
Famine alters social behaviour passed to grandchildren culturally

items.reveal_title: Heijmans, Tobi and colleagues — the Hongerwinter epigenetic study
items.reveal:
Heijmans et al. (2008) compared DNA methylation in adults who had been in utero during the Dutch famine to their unexposed siblings. The famine-exposed showed less methylation at the IGF2 gene 60 years later.

More recent work has shown some methylation marks pass to grandchildren, with associated health correlates.

This is not classical Lamarckism (inheritance of acquired characteristics through soft inheritance). Methylation marks are mostly cleared between generations, but some escape erasure. The mechanisms are still being mapped.

Distinguishing real intergenerational inheritance from confounders (in utero exposure, shared environment) requires careful study design. Animal models (rodents) have been used to confirm causal mechanisms.
items.why: Inheritance is taught as DNA sequence transmission. Some heritable information is encoded above the sequence, in modifications to DNA and chromatin — and famine can leave its mark across decades.

items.title: Bacteria count themselves before acting
items.claim: A single Vibrio fischeri bacterium doesn't glow. A dense colony of them lights up the inside of squid light organs and certain Hawaiian fish. The bacteria sense how many bacteria are around them and only switch on bioluminescence when there are enough to matter.
items.prompt: How does a bacterium know how many others are nearby?

options.text: They count visually
Quorum sensing — each cell secretes a small molecule (an autoinducer); local concentration of autoinducer rises with population density, and at threshold activates gene expression
They listen for vibrations
They wait a fixed time before turning on

items.reveal:
Quorum sensing was discovered in Vibrio fischeri by Hastings and Nealson in the 1970s. Each bacterium continuously produces and secretes a homoserine lactone. At low cell density it diffuses away; at high density it accumulates, enters cells and binds a transcription factor that activates luciferase genes.

Bonnie Bassler's group showed in the 1990s that many bacteria use multiple quorum signals — one species-specific, one universal (AI-2). The universal one allows cross-species 'eavesdropping' on population density of other bacteria.

Pathogens use quorum sensing to time virulence factor expression: stay quiet until there are enough cells to overwhelm the host. Anti-quorum-sensing drugs are an active research area for antibiotic alternatives.
items.why: Bacteria are imagined as solitary cells acting independently. Many of their key behaviours — virulence, biofilm formation, bioluminescence — are coordinated through chemical signalling networks.

items.title: A tumour is a tiny evolving ecosystem
items.claim: Cancer cells accumulate mutations. Cells with mutations that confer growth advantages dominate. Drug treatment kills the susceptible cells but spares resistant ones — which then dominate the regrown tumour.
items.prompt: Why is cancer so hard to cure even with effective drugs?

options.text: Drugs don't work on cancer cells

A tumour contains millions to billions of slightly genetically different cells; selection pressure from a drug acts on the existing variation and rapidly enriches resistant clones — the same evolutionary process as antibiotic resistance, but inside a single patient
Cancer cells repair themselves
The immune system always fails

items.reveal_title: Tumour heterogeneity and the cost of monotherapy
items.reveal:
Single-cell sequencing of tumours reveals enormous clonal diversity. A 5 cm tumour may contain 10 to the 9 cells, each with its own profile of acquired mutations. Subclones can have different drug sensitivities, growth rates and metastatic potentials.

Treating with a single targeted therapy selects for whichever cells are pre-existingly resistant. Within months, the tumour regrows — now dominated by the resistant subclone. Combination therapy (targeting multiple pathways at once) makes resistance much less likely, by analogy with HIV's HAART protocol.

The Peter Nowell paper (1976) first proposed clonal evolution in cancer. Recent decades have made it the dominant framework, with implications for drug strategy, biomarker design, and the inevitability of resistance.
items.why: Cancer is taught as one disease. It's an evolving population of cells subject to selection — making it as much an ecological and evolutionary problem as a medical one.

items.title: Most adult humans can't digest milk — and that's normal
items.claim: Babies make lactase to digest lactose in milk. In most of the world's adults, lactase production switches off after weaning. Adult milk-drinkers — common in Europeans and some African and Middle Eastern populations — carry a recently evolved mutation.
items.prompt: Which is the 'normal' human state?

options.text: Adult lactose tolerance
Adult lactose intolerance is ancestral; lactase persistence is a derived trait that arose in populations that domesticated dairy animals in the last 10,000 years
All humans are lactose-intolerant
All humans are lactose-tolerant

items.reveal:
Roughly 65 percent of adult humans globally show reduced lactase production after weaning. Lactase persistence is most common in northern Europeans (around 90 percent), some West African pastoralist groups, and some Middle Eastern populations.

Different regulatory mutations independently produced this trait in different lineages — convergent evolution. The European variant (a single nucleotide change near the LCT gene, called T-13910) is dated to about 5,000 to 10,000 years ago, coinciding with cattle domestication.

Dairy farming and lactase persistence appear to have co-evolved: ancient DNA shows farmers drank milk before persistence was common, suggesting cultural use (fermented dairy, lower lactose) preceded biological adaptation. As populations relied more on milk, the persistence allele was strongly selected.
items.why: European diets are taken as a baseline; lactose intolerance is treated as a disorder. Globally, lactose intolerance IS the baseline — milk drinking adults are the rare ones.

items.title: You are paralysed multiple times every night
items.claim: During REM sleep, when most dreams occur, motor neurons to your skeletal muscles are actively inhibited. You cannot move. This is REM atonia — and when it fails, people act out their dreams.
items.prompt: Why does the brain paralyse you while dreaming?

options.text: To conserve energy
To prevent acting out dream content — the same brain regions that command movement are active in REM as in waking, but spinal motor neurons are blocked from receiving the signals
To stop heart rate from rising
To allow muscles to repair

items.reveal_title: REM behavior disorder and Schenck's discovery
items.reveal:
The brainstem (specifically the pons and medulla) sends inhibitory signals to spinal motor neurons during REM. The motor cortex fires in patterns resembling waking; the descending commands reach the spinal cord but cannot trigger muscle contraction.

In REM Behavior Disorder (Schenck 1986), this paralysis fails. Patients punch, kick, vocalise and act out vivid dreams. RBD is strongly associated with later Parkinson's disease and Lewy body dementia — the brainstem regions controlling REM atonia degrade early in these conditions.

Narcolepsy with cataplexy is the opposite failure: REM-style atonia intrudes into waking life, triggered by emotion. Modafinil and other treatments stabilise the boundary between sleep states.
items.why: Sleep is imagined as 'off'. REM sleep is intensely active — and the body needs active suppression to prevent the brain's instructions reaching the muscles.

items.title: Snapdragons disprove Mendel's simplest law in one cross
items.claim: Red snapdragon crossed with white snapdragon. Mendel's dominance rule says: offspring should all be red (or all white). Snapdragon offspring are PINK. The textbook law fails on its very first test.
items.prompt: What's going on?

options.text: Mendel's laws don't apply to plants

Incomplete dominance — heterozygotes show an intermediate phenotype because neither allele fully masks the other; the red allele encodes a pigment enzyme, and one functional copy produces only half as much pigment as two
Pink is a separate allele not from either parent
Mutations occurred during the cross

items.reveal:
Mendel happened to choose seven traits in peas that were all controlled by single genes with full dominance and complete penetrance. Most real traits are not.

Incomplete dominance: heterozygotes show intermediate phenotypes. Pink snapdragons. Pink camellias. Light pink human skin (one functional MC1R copy).

Codominance: both alleles fully expressed simultaneously. Human ABO blood group (a person with A and B alleles has both A and B antigens on red cells).

Epistasis: gene A's effect depends on gene B's genotype. Coat colour in Labradors (E gene controls whether B gene's brown/black is visible at all).

Polygenic inheritance: traits like height controlled by hundreds of small-effect genes. Family resemblance plus 'regression to the mean'.

Real genetics is much richer than 'dominant masks recessive'.
items.why: Mendel's laws are presented as universal. They describe a subset of inheritance patterns. Even simple breeding shows the laws don't always apply directly.

items.title: The oxygen you breathe comes from WATER, not CO2
items.claim: Photosynthesis takes in CO2 and water and produces sugar and oxygen. Every chemistry student writes the equation. But the O2 released is not stripped from the CO2 — it comes entirely from splitting water molecules.
items.prompt: How do we know the oxygen comes from water?

options.text: Both water and CO2 contribute oxygen equally
Ruben and Kamen (1941) used the heavy isotope oxygen-18 to label either water or CO2; the released O2 carried the label only when the water was labelled, never when the CO2 was
CO2 is the source of the oxygen
The oxygen comes from chlorophyll

items.reveal:
The light reactions of photosynthesis split water (photolysis) at the oxygen-evolving complex — a manganese-calcium cluster in Photosystem II. Two water molecules are split: 2 H2O -> 4 H+ + 4 e- + O2.

The electrons enter the electron transport chain. The protons contribute to the thylakoid pH gradient (lumen reaches pH ~5, stroma ~8). ATP synthase uses the gradient to make ATP.

The Calvin cycle (in the stroma) uses ATP and NADPH to fix CO2 into sugar. The carbon from CO2 becomes the carbon in glucose. But the oxygen atoms in CO2 mostly end up in carbohydrate, NOT in the released O2.

Oxygen is, from photosynthesis's point of view, a waste product — and arguably the most consequential pollution event in Earth's history (the Great Oxidation Event, ~2.4 billion years ago, killed most anaerobic life).
items.why: The arrow-pushing equation suggests CO2 donates oxygen. The actual chemistry inverts that: water is split, CO2 is reduced, and the oxygen you breathe was once dissolved in a chloroplast.

items.title: Every leaf contains the descendants of a captured bacterium
items.claim: Chloroplasts have their own circular DNA, their own ribosomes, a double membrane, and divide by fission. About 1.5 billion years ago, a eukaryotic cell engulfed a cyanobacterium and kept it as a permanent tenant.
items.prompt: What's the strongest single line of evidence?

options.text: Chloroplasts are green
Chloroplast 16S ribosomal RNA sequences group phylogenetically with free-living cyanobacteria, not with any eukaryotic structure — they are bacterial by descent
Chloroplasts can be removed without killing the plant
They contain pigments

items.reveal:
The original engulfment (primary endosymbiosis) gave rise to the chloroplasts of red algae, green algae and land plants. The cyanobacterial guest lost most of its genome to the host nucleus over time, but retained ~120 genes — mostly for photosynthesis machinery.

Later, secondary endosymbiosis occurred: a non-photosynthetic eukaryote engulfed a red or green alga. The result is the four-membraned plastids of diatoms, brown algae, and apicomplexans (the parasites that cause malaria still carry a vestigial non-photosynthetic plastid).

The apicoplast in Plasmodium is a drug target — anti-bacterial drugs (clindamycin, doxycycline) kill malaria parasites by poisoning their plastid's bacterial-style ribosomes.

Lynn Margulis pushed endosymbiosis from a fringe idea to consensus. Without it, photosynthesis would never have entered eukaryotic life.
items.why: Plant cells feel monolithic. They are chimeras — green parts of every leaf descend from a captured bacterium that never left.

items.title: Pineapples photosynthesise at night
items.claim: Most plants open their stomata in daytime to take in CO2 and lose water to evaporation. CAM plants (crassulacean acid metabolism — cacti, pineapples, agaves) keep stomata SHUT all day and open them only at night, storing CO2 as malic acid for the day's photosynthesis.
items.prompt: Why would a plant fix CO2 in the dark?

options.text: Light isn't needed for photosynthesis
By separating CO2 uptake (cool, humid night) from light reactions (hot, dry day), CAM plants cut water loss by 80-90% versus C3 plants — essential in deserts where transpiration would be lethal
Nighttime CO2 is more abundant
Light damages the CO2-fixing enzyme

items.reveal:
C3 plants (wheat, rice, ~85% of species): Rubisco fixes CO2 directly in mesophyll cells. Simple, but loses water and suffers photorespiration when hot.

C4 plants (maize, sugarcane, sorghum): PEP carboxylase fixes CO2 into a 4-carbon acid (oxaloacetate) in mesophyll cells. The acid is shipped to bundle-sheath cells, where Rubisco operates in a CO2-rich environment. About 3% of species, but include some of the most productive crops.

CAM plants (cacti, pineapples, succulents, agaves): same chemistry as C4 but separated in TIME instead of space. Stomata open at night; CO2 is stored as malic acid in vacuoles; daylight releases it for Rubisco.

Each is a different trade-off between water loss, productivity and temperature tolerance. C4 and CAM evolved independently dozens of times — convergent solutions to Rubisco's flaws.
items.why: Photosynthesis is taught as a single process. In reality, plants have invented three biochemically distinct strategies, each suited to a different climate.

items.title: Trees pull water up under tension that could split steel
items.claim: A 100-metre redwood lifts water from roots to crown without any pump. The xylem column is under NEGATIVE pressure (tension) of -1 to -2 megapascals — enough to cavitate steel cables. The water column holds because of cohesion between water molecules.
items.prompt: What pulls the water up?

options.text: Root pressure pushes from below

Evaporation at the leaf surface pulls on the continuous water column; cohesion (hydrogen bonds between water molecules) plus adhesion to xylem walls transmits the tension all the way to the roots — the cohesion-tension theory (Dixon & Joly, 1894)
Photosynthesis chemically pumps water upward
Gravity reverses inside plants

items.reveal_title: The tallest pump that isn't a pump
items.reveal:
Atmospheric pressure can only lift water about 10 metres against a vacuum. So redwoods aren't being pushed from below — they are being PULLED from above.

Evaporation at leaf stomata creates a curved water meniscus. Surface tension at this meniscus reduces pressure in the underlying xylem to less than zero (real negative pressure, not just sub-atmospheric). Hydrogen bonds between water molecules keep the column intact under tension.

If the tension breaks, you get cavitation: a bubble forms and the column ruptures. Trees minimise this by having millions of redundant narrow xylem vessels.

The theoretical maximum height for a tree, set by cavitation risk and gravitational pull on the water, is about 130 metres. The tallest known tree, Hyperion (a coast redwood), is 115.7 metres — close to the physical limit.
items.why: Pumps push. Trees pull — and the pulling reaches pressures so negative they should rip the liquid apart. The molecular cohesion of water is one of biology's most exploited features.

items.title: Stomata are tiny mouths that decide between starving and drying
items.claim: A leaf has hundreds of stomata per square millimetre. Open them: CO2 enters for photosynthesis but water evaporates away. Close them: water is saved but photosynthesis stalls. Plants must decide minute by minute.
items.prompt: How do guard cells open and close the stomatal pore?

options.text: Tiny muscles contract
Guard cells actively pump K+ ions in; water follows by osmosis; the cell swells; thicker inner walls force the cell to bow outward, opening the pore. Reverse the process to close
Heat physically expands them
The stomata are always open

items.reveal:
Each stoma is bordered by two guard cells. Their inner walls (facing the pore) are thicker and less elastic than their outer walls.

Opening: blue light activates a proton pump (H+-ATPase). The cells become more negative inside; K+ flows in via channels. Cl- and malate follow. Water enters by osmosis. Turgor rises. The thinner outer walls expand more than the inner walls, pulling the cells apart and opening the pore.

Closing: ABA (abscisic acid, the drought-stress hormone) triggers K+ efflux. The cells lose water and shrink. The pore closes.

Most plants close stomata at night (no photosynthesis needed) and during drought. CAM plants invert this. Wheat loses ~500 kg of water per kg of grain produced — most through stomata.

Climate change is forcing plants to evolve stomatal density: rising CO2 lets leaves get the same carbon with fewer stomata, reducing water loss.
items.why: Stomatal regulation is the central trade-off of land plant life. Engineering stomata for higher water-use efficiency is a major target of crop science.

items.title: You synthesise your body weight in ATP every day
items.claim: ATP is the cell's energy currency. Your body contains only about 50 grams at any moment, but you turn it over so fast that you make and consume the equivalent of your full body mass — 60 to 80 kilograms — daily.
items.prompt: How can a tiny pool turn over so much?

options.text: ATP makes copies of itself
Each ATP molecule is hydrolysed and re-synthesised hundreds of times per day; mitochondria continuously rebuild ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate using the proton motive force from respiration
Most of the body's mass is ATP
ATP is consumed only during exercise

items.reveal:
An adult at rest uses about 2000 kcal per day. Each ATP hydrolysis releases ~7.3 kcal/mol of free energy under standard conditions, more under cellular conditions.

Working through: ~65 kg of ATP cycled per day, give or take. Each molecule of ATP cycles roughly 1000-1500 times daily.

The cell stores essentially no ATP for emergencies. It maintains a flux instead. Stop respiration and your ATP pool depletes in seconds — which is exactly why cyanide is so fast.

Muscles store some quick-access energy as phosphocreatine (a few seconds of all-out sprint) and glycogen (~minutes), but ATP itself is continuously regenerated, not stockpiled.

This is metabolism's deep design choice: a small, dynamic currency pool, refilled by continuous oxidation of food.
items.why: Energy storage feels like the obvious solution. Cells went the other way — keep almost no ATP, rebuild it constantly. The flux IS the metabolism.

items.title: Babies have a special fat that wastes energy as heat — on purpose
items.claim: Brown adipose tissue, found in newborns and hibernating mammals, contains mitochondria packed with a protein (UCP1) that lets protons leak back across the inner membrane WITHOUT making ATP. The energy is dissipated as pure heat.
items.prompt: Why deliberately uncouple respiration from ATP synthesis?

options.text: It's a mistake the body cannot fix
Newborns and small mammals lose heat fast (high surface area to volume ratio). Brown fat lets them generate large amounts of heat on demand without shivering — burning fat directly to warmth
UCP1 makes extra ATP
It cools the body

items.reveal:
In ordinary mitochondria, the electron transport chain pumps protons OUT; ATP synthase lets them back IN, capturing the energy as ATP.

In brown adipose tissue, the protein UCP1 (uncoupling protein 1, also called thermogenin) provides an alternative route for protons to flow back in — bypassing ATP synthase. The proton gradient still forms; the energy still flows; but it dissipates as heat rather than ATP.

Brown fat is brown because it's packed with mitochondria (iron-rich cytochromes). It's especially abundant in newborn humans (around the neck and shoulder blades) and in hibernating mammals (which use it to wake from torpor).

Adults retain some brown fat, more in lean people; PET-CT scans light it up. There's active research into pharmacologically activating brown fat as an anti-obesity strategy.

The drug DNP (2,4-dinitrophenol) chemically uncouples mitochondria. It does cause weight loss — but also fatal hyperthermia. It's been banned for human use for nearly a century, though it still kills bodybuilders occasionally.
items.why: Inefficiency seems like a flaw. The body uses controlled mitochondrial inefficiency as a thermostat — and biotech is trying to weaponise it against obesity.

items.title: Sprinting and marathon running use chemically different fuels
items.claim: Aerobic respiration of one glucose produces about 30-32 ATP. Anaerobic glycolysis produces only 2 ATP. Yet sprinters rely on the anaerobic path. Why use a pathway that wastes 94% of glucose's chemical energy?
items.prompt: Why ever choose anaerobic?

options.text: It's faster — sprint muscle can produce ATP via glycolysis ~100x faster per second than oxidative phosphorylation can. Power output wins over efficiency in short bursts
Anaerobic respiration is more efficient
Oxygen is poisonous to muscles
Anaerobic is the only option

items.reveal:
Aerobic respiration is the efficient long path: glycolysis (cytoplasm) -> pyruvate -> Krebs cycle (mitochondrial matrix) -> oxidative phosphorylation -> ~30-32 ATP per glucose, with CO2 and water as byproducts.

Anaerobic glycolysis stops at pyruvate, converts it to lactate (regenerating the NAD+ glycolysis needs), and quits. Yield: 2 ATP per glucose. But it runs without oxygen and at ~100x the rate of mitochondrial ATP synthesis.

Sprint events (100m, weightlifting): mostly anaerobic. Lactate builds up. Burns. The 'oxygen debt' you owe after sprinting is the cost of clearing the lactate and replenishing phosphocreatine.

Endurance events (marathon, cycling): mostly aerobic, fuelled by glucose at first, then fat. Fat yields ~106 ATP per palmitate molecule but is metabolised slowly — fine for steady output.

Yeasts do alcoholic fermentation (pyruvate -> ethanol + CO2) instead of lactate fermentation. Same logic: regenerate NAD+ and keep glycolysis running when oxygen runs low.
items.why: Efficiency seems obviously best. For peak power, throughput beats efficiency every time — which is why sprinters look chemically different from marathoners during a race.

items.title: Your cell membranes are 200,000 volts per centimetre
items.claim: The inner mitochondrial membrane has a voltage of about 150 mV across its 5-nanometre thickness. Scaled up, that's an electric field of 30 million volts per metre — strong enough to ionise air. Cells run their lives in fields this intense.
items.prompt: Why is the membrane voltage so high?

options.text: It's an accident of evolution

The proton motive force has two components — pH gradient (~1 unit) and electrical potential (~150 mV) — and together they store the energy released by respiration in a form that ATP synthase can harvest
Mitochondria conduct electricity for the cell
Voltage is needed for genetic material to fold

items.reveal:
Peter Mitchell's chemiosmotic theory unified electron transport with ATP synthesis through the proton motive force (PMF). Total PMF (the cell's 'fuel gauge') = chemical potential of proton gradient + electrical potential of charge separation.

Magnitudes in mitochondria: pH gradient is about 0.7 units (intermembrane space more acidic), membrane potential about -150 to -180 mV (matrix is negative). Together: ~200 mV of PMF, or ~20 kJ/mol of proton transferred.

The field strength (~3 x 10^7 V/m) inside the membrane is comparable to lightning. Life happens at electric fields that humans only experience during catastrophes.

Across thylakoid membranes (chloroplasts), the gradient is mostly chemical (pH 5 vs 8) rather than electrical.

Disrupting PMF with uncouplers, ionophores or cyanide kills cells in seconds — the gradient must be continuously rebuilt to maintain ATP synthesis.
items.why: Cells seem soft and slow. The energy machinery within them runs at field strengths that would shatter rigid materials. Life depends on holding lightning-scale electricity inside membranes of fat.

items.title: Reintroducing wolves changed the course of rivers in Yellowstone
items.claim: Grey wolves were exterminated from Yellowstone by 1926. In 1995, 14 wolves were reintroduced. Within 20 years, elk populations dropped, willows and aspen regrew along riverbanks, beaver populations rose, and river channels narrowed.
items.prompt: How can predators reshape rivers?

options.text: Wolves physically dig riverbanks

A trophic cascade: wolves reduce elk numbers and (especially) keep them moving, releasing browse pressure on streamside trees, which stabilise banks. The effect propagates through multiple trophic levels
Wolves drink large amounts of river water
It's coincidence — climate change did it

items.reveal:
The Yellowstone story is the textbook trophic cascade. Wolves don't only kill elk; they shift elk behaviour — herds avoid areas where they can't see predators coming, like valley bottoms with dense vegetation.

Released from constant browsing, willows and aspens regrow. Beavers, which need willows, return — by 2014, beaver colonies had increased from 1 to 9. Beaver dams trap sediment, raise water tables, create wetlands.

The full claim ('wolves changed the rivers') is contested. William Ripple and Robert Beschta documented the vegetation rebound; Arthur Middleton and others argue confounding factors (climate, bear predation, elk hunting outside the park) explain much of it.

What is uncontroversial: keystone species have effects on ecosystems vastly out of proportion to their biomass. Sea otters and kelp forests, starfish and intertidal communities, sharks and seagrass — similar cascades documented worldwide.

Keystone species concept: Robert Paine (1969), who removed starfish from a Pacific Northwest tide pool and watched it collapse to a mussel monoculture.
items.why: Ecosystems are imagined as bottom-up: plants determine herbivores determine carnivores. Top predators flip the picture — top-down control is real, and big effects can come from species with little biomass.

items.title: Sea otters maintain entire underwater forests
items.claim: Where sea otters live, kelp forests thrive. Where they have been hunted to near-extinction, sea urchins explode and graze kelp to bare rock ('urchin barrens'). One otter eats about 25% of its body mass in urchins daily.
items.prompt: What makes otters a keystone species?

options.text: They are the largest predators present
They selectively eat sea urchins, the only major kelp grazer in the system; removing otters releases urchin populations, which devastate kelp forests that support hundreds of other species
Otters fertilise the water with their waste
Otters physically prop up kelp

items.reveal:
Jim Estes and John Palmisano (1974) compared Aleutian islands with otters to islands where otters had been wiped out for the fur trade. The contrast was startling: lush kelp forests vs barren urchin-grazed rock.

Kelp forests are enormously productive. They support fish, invertebrates, sea birds, marine mammals. They sequester carbon. They dampen wave energy and protect coasts.

Subsequent work (Estes et al. 1998) suggested that killer whale predation on sea otters — possibly because their normal prey, large whales, had been depleted by whaling — was driving a SECOND collapse of Aleutian otter populations, with knock-on collapses of kelp.

A whaling-era extinction cascade may still be propagating decades later. Ecosystems have memory.

The 'keystone species' concept (Paine 1969) was based on starfish; otters became its most famous illustration. Many ecosystems have keystones; identifying them before they collapse is a recurring conservation challenge.
items.why: Big effects from one species seem improbable. In sea otter ecosystems, the entire architecture depends on one mid-sized predator preventing one herbivore from grazing the forest down.

items.title: Lions get only 0.001% of the sun's energy that hit their grass
items.claim: Each trophic level passes about 10% of its energy to the next. Sun -> grass -> antelope -> lion. Three steps means lions retain 0.1% of grass energy. Add another step and you're down to 0.01%. The tenth-of-energy rule explains why food chains are short.
items.prompt: Where does the missing 90% go?

options.text: Stored as fat

Most of the consumed energy goes to respiration (powering the consumer's metabolism), heat loss, and undigested waste; only a small fraction is converted into new tissue available to the next predator
Locked into DNA and proteins
Reflected back as light

items.reveal:
Raymond Lindeman (1942) measured energy flow in Cedar Bog Lake, Minnesota. He found progressive losses at each trophic level — formalising 'trophic efficiency'.

Typical values: primary producers fix ~1-2% of incident solar energy as net primary productivity. Herbivores extract ~10% of plant productivity. Carnivores ~10% of herbivore productivity. Top predators get a tiny fraction of the original solar input.

Consequences: food chains rarely exceed 4-5 trophic levels; predators have huge home ranges and small populations; ecosystems with apex predators are inherently fragile to disruption at the base.

The '10% rule' is an approximation. Efficiencies actually vary: ectotherms (fish, reptiles) can transfer 30-40% because they don't spend energy maintaining body heat. Endotherms (mammals, birds) burn most of what they eat to stay warm.

Vegetarian arguments often invoke this: feeding plants directly to people is ~10x more energy-efficient than routing them through livestock first.
items.why: Food chains feel boundless. Thermodynamics caps them at 4 or 5 links. Each predator carries the entropic cost of every prey it ate.

items.title: Lakes flip between two stable states with no warning
items.claim: A clear lake with submerged plants can — if nutrient loading exceeds a threshold — suddenly transform into a green, turbid lake dominated by algae. The shift is rapid, hard to reverse, and almost impossible to predict from gradual measurements.
items.prompt: What's happening at the tipping point?

options.text: The lake's temperature rises
Positive feedback loops (algae shade out plants; sediment resuspends; phosphorus releases from anoxic sediments) take over once a threshold is crossed; the new state then reinforces itself
The lake's bottom collapses
Nothing — the shift is gradual

items.reveal_title: Marten Scheffer and alternative stable states
items.reveal:
Marten Scheffer and colleagues (Nature 2001, 2009) formalised the concept of alternative stable states in ecology. Many ecosystems can sit in one of two (or more) regimes, with sharp transitions between them.

A shallow lake's clear regime: rooted plants stabilise sediment; light penetrates; zooplankton eat algae. The turbid regime: algae bloom; light is blocked; plants die; bottom-feeding fish stir up sediment; phosphorus releases from anoxic mud; algae get more nutrient. Each state reinforces itself.

Loading a clear lake with phosphorus may have NO obvious effect — until a threshold is crossed. Then it flips fast. Reducing phosphorus AFTER the flip rarely restores the clear state directly; the lake stays turbid because the turbid state's feedback loops are now in charge. You may need to remove fish, biomanipulate, or wait years.

Similar regime shifts: coral reef to algal mat, savannah to desert (Sahara, 5500 BC), tundra to forest.

Early-warning signals (slowing recovery from perturbations, rising variance) precede tipping points by months to decades, but are subtle and contested.
items.why: Slow change feels safe. Real ecosystems can absorb stress invisibly for years and then collapse to a new state in months. The signal you want comes after the threshold is crossed.

items.title: Species are vanishing 100 to 1000 times faster than normal
items.claim: The fossil record gives a 'background' extinction rate: roughly 1 species per million per year. Current rates are 100 to 1000 times that — and rising. Many biologists call it the sixth mass extinction.
items.prompt: What's the main driver?

options.text: Asteroid impact like 66 million years ago
Habitat destruction (especially tropical deforestation), invasive species, climate change, pollution and overharvesting — a multi-cause anthropogenic mass extinction with no single dominant mechanism
Volcanic eruptions
Natural background extinction unchanged

items.reveal:
The five previous mass extinctions (Ordovician, Devonian, Permian, Triassic, Cretaceous) each saw 50-95% of species disappear over geological timescales. The Permian was the worst — ~96% of marine species lost over ~60,000 years.

The current rate, calculated from documented vertebrate extinctions (Ceballos, Ehrlich and others), is 100-1000 times background. Insect biomass declines (Hallmann et al. 2017, Krefeld study) show 75% reductions over 27 years in German nature reserves.

Human impacts: forest cover reduced by ~30% globally since 1700; ocean fish biomass down ~50% since 1970; freshwater vertebrates down 84% (WWF Living Planet Report). Climate change adds an accelerating layer.

Protected areas and conservation work — by some measures, extinction rates would have been 4x higher without them.

Mass extinctions reshape evolution for tens of millions of years. We won't return to the world we know within human-relevant timeframes — the species we lose are lost.
items.why: Species loss feels gradual. The rate is geological in magnitude — comparable to events that left fossil-record-defining boundaries. We are living through one.

items.title: Your kidneys filter 180 litres of blood plasma every day
items.claim: Each kidney has about a million nephrons. Together they filter 125 ml of plasma per minute — 180 litres per day. Your final urine output is 1 to 2 litres. The kidneys reabsorb 99% of what they filter.
items.prompt: Why filter so much only to put it back?

options.text: The kidneys are inefficient

Bulk filtration is the only way to expose all blood-borne solutes to selective reabsorption; the kidney keeps what's needed (glucose, salts, amino acids, water) and lets the rest go — fine selectivity requires high throughput
The body has extra water to spare
Filtration prevents kidney stones

items.reveal:
The glomerulus is a knot of capillaries inside a Bowman's capsule. Blood pressure forces plasma (minus proteins and cells) through a selective barrier into the nephron tubule.

Flow rates: glomerular filtration rate (GFR) ~120-125 ml/min in healthy adults. Total renal blood flow ~1.2 L/min — about 20-25% of cardiac output. The kidneys take a major share of the circulation for their mass.

The filtrate then passes through the tubules. Proximal tubule reabsorbs glucose, amino acids, most salts, water. Loop of Henle sets up an osmotic gradient. Distal tubule fine-tunes. Collecting duct adjusts water under ADH (antidiuretic hormone).

Result: 180 L filtered, 178.5 L returned to blood, 1.5 L excreted as urine.

GFR drops with age (~1% per year after 40), kidney disease, dehydration. Maintaining it is why drinking water matters — and why drugs that affect kidney function require careful monitoring.
items.why: Filtration that throws everything out and re-claims most of it sounds wasteful. It's the simplest design that ensures any potentially harmful blood-borne molecule eventually leaves the body.

items.title: Your lungs have the surface area of half a tennis court
items.claim: Two lungs, about 4 to 6 litres total volume — but the internal surface area where gas exchange happens is 50 to 75 square metres. Achieved by 300 to 500 million alveoli, each a tiny sphere with a thin shared wall to a capillary.
items.prompt: Why is so much surface area needed?

options.text: To make breathing audible

Diffusion of gases across a membrane scales with surface area and inversely with thickness; meeting the body's O2 demand (~250 ml/min at rest, ~3 L/min at exercise) requires both a huge area and an ultra-thin barrier (~0.5 micrometres)
Extra alveoli are spare in case some collapse
To filter dust

items.reveal:
Rate of diffusion = (surface area * concentration gradient) / (membrane thickness). To maximise O2 uptake, organisms maximise area, maximise gradient (high O2 in air vs low in blood) and minimise thickness.

Alveoli: 0.2-0.5 mm diameter spheres, lined with type I cells (extremely thin), surrounded by capillaries. The blood-air barrier is only 2-3 cells thick — sometimes <0.5 micrometres.

If you flattened all alveoli out, they would cover ~70 square metres — close to a singles tennis court.

Diseases that destroy alveoli (emphysema) reduce gas exchange capacity. Pulmonary fibrosis thickens the barrier. Both cause shortness of breath at exertion.

Total lung capillary blood volume is only ~75 ml at rest, but blood transits in ~0.75 seconds — enough for full equilibration in healthy lungs. At maximal exercise, transit time can drop to 0.25 seconds; in well-trained athletes at altitude, diffusion can become rate-limiting.
items.why: Big surface in small volume seems like a packaging miracle. Evolution solved it with tessellated bubbles — and made breathing possible at human body size.

items.title: Your heart pumps 7000 litres of blood every day
items.claim: Resting heart rate ~70 bpm. Stroke volume ~70 ml. Cardiac output ~5 litres per minute, 7200 litres per day. Over an average lifetime: 250 million litres pumped — enough to fill 100 Olympic swimming pools.
items.prompt: How can such a small muscle pump so much?

options.text: The heart is hollow so volume doesn't matter

Continuous high turnover: each heartbeat moves a small volume, but ~100,000 beats per day add up; cardiac muscle is uniquely adapted (intercalated discs, dense mitochondria, near-zero anaerobic capacity) to never tire
Most of the volume is recycled within the heart
Blood is much lighter than water

items.reveal:
Cardiac muscle (myocardium) is structurally distinct from skeletal muscle. Cells are short, branching, with one or two nuclei, joined by intercalated discs containing gap junctions that synchronise contraction.

About 30% of cardiac muscle volume is mitochondria (vs 1-2% in skeletal muscle). The heart oxidises fatty acids preferentially and never fatigues under normal conditions.

It's also self-rhythmic: the sinoatrial node (in the right atrium) generates 70-80 spontaneous depolarisations per minute, propagated via the AV node and Purkinje fibres. Cut all nerves to the heart and it keeps beating (just at a different rate).

Under exercise, cardiac output can rise to 25+ L/min (5x resting) — by increasing both heart rate and stroke volume. Elite athletes have larger left ventricles and lower resting heart rates (40s, even 30s).

The heart's own coronary arteries feed it. Block one and the muscle downstream dies in minutes — myocardial infarction.
items.why: Continuous lifelong pumping sounds impossible. Heart muscle isn't ordinary muscle — it's a specialised contractile tissue evolved precisely never to stop.

items.title: Your blood vessels stretched end to end would circle Earth twice
items.claim: The human body contains about 100,000 kilometres of blood vessels, almost all of which is capillaries. Earth's equator is 40,075 km. Two and a half wraps.
items.prompt: How is so much vessel length packed inside a person?

options.text: Most vessels are extremely thin

Capillaries are ~5-10 micrometres in diameter — they pass red blood cells in single file. Their tiny cross-section means enormous total length fits in tissue, while still leaving most tissue volume for cells
Vessels run in spirals to fit
Most vessels are gas-filled tubes

items.reveal:
Aorta: ~2.5 cm diameter, 1 metre long. Branches into arteries, arterioles, then capillaries. Capillaries number ~10 billion in the body, total length ~80,000-100,000 km.

Almost every cell is within ~50 micrometres of a capillary — the maximum diffusion distance for oxygen. This drives the geometry: dense, thin, ramifying vessels.

Total cross-sectional area increases at each branching level: aorta ~5 cm^2, all capillaries combined ~4000 cm^2. By the conservation equation (flow = velocity * area), blood velocity drops from ~30 cm/s in the aorta to ~0.1 cm/s in capillaries — allowing time for diffusion.

Vascular networks follow allometric scaling laws (West, Brown, Enquist) that approximate optimal transport — minimising energy cost of moving blood. The same scaling rules describe trees, river networks, urban roads.

New capillary formation (angiogenesis) is closely controlled. Tumours hijack it to grow blood supply; anti-angiogenic drugs (bevacizumab) starve them.
items.why: A circulatory system 100,000 km long sounds external. It's packed inside a human body because each capillary is a fraction of a hair wide — and there are billions of them.

items.title: Your core temperature varies by less than 1 degree all day
items.claim: Air temperature swings by 30 degrees C between Australian outback day and night. Sahara desert: 50 C day, 0 C night. Yet healthy human core temperature stays at 36.5-37.5 C across these extremes. We are walking thermostats.
items.prompt: How does the body hold core temperature constant?

options.text: The skin acts as insulation only

Negative feedback through the hypothalamus: sensors monitor core temperature; effectors include sweating (cooling), vasodilation/vasoconstriction (heat dump or retention), shivering (heat production), and behavioural responses (seek shade, put on clothes)
Body heat is generated constantly at the same rate
Hair traps heat passively

items.reveal:
The preoptic area of the hypothalamus contains warm-sensitive and cold-sensitive neurons. They integrate skin temperature (peripheral) and blood temperature (core) and adjust effector outputs.

When too hot: blood vessels in skin dilate; sweat glands release ~0.5-1.5 L/hour (up to 3 L/hour in heat-acclimated athletes); behaviour (seek shade).

When too cold: skin vessels constrict; shivering (involuntary skeletal muscle activity, heat output up to 5x resting); brown fat thermogenesis (less in adults); piloerection (goose bumps — useless on hairless humans but works in furred mammals); behaviour (seek shelter).

Fever is a deliberately raised set-point — the hypothalamus is told (by pyrogens) that 38.5 C is the new target. Your body now defends 38.5 the way it usually defends 37.

Heatstroke: thermoregulation fails at core temperatures above ~40 C. Mortality rises rapidly. Conversely, deep hypothermia (<30 C) shuts down cardiac function — but has been used surgically to extend safe ischemia times.

The set-point isn't constant: circadian variation (~0.5 C lower at night), menstrual cycle (~0.3 C higher post-ovulation), age-related decline in regulation precision.
items.why: Homeostasis is usually drawn as a circle on a board. It's an integration of dozens of mechanisms across the whole body — and breaks down in fascinating ways (fever, heatstroke, hypothermia) when stressed.

items.title: Your blood sugar is regulated within a 30% range despite irregular meals
items.claim: Normal fasting blood glucose: 4-6 mmol/L. After a meal: rises to 7-8, then back to baseline within 2 hours. Healthy people maintain this range whether they eat constantly or fast for a day.
items.prompt: What hormones drive the regulation?

options.text: Adrenaline only

Insulin (from pancreatic beta cells) lowers blood glucose by promoting uptake and storage; glucagon (from alpha cells) raises it by mobilising stored glycogen — a classic antagonistic pair under negative feedback
The liver alone controls glucose
The brain regulates glucose mechanically

items.reveal:
After a meal: blood glucose rises. Beta cells in the pancreas detect it via glucokinase and secrete insulin. Insulin tells muscle and fat to take up glucose, and the liver to store it as glycogen.

Between meals: glucose drops. Alpha cells secrete glucagon. Glucagon tells the liver to break down glycogen and release glucose into the blood. If glycogen runs out (after ~24 hours fasting), gluconeogenesis from amino acids and glycerol takes over.

Type 1 diabetes: autoimmune destruction of beta cells. No insulin. Blood glucose unregulated. Discovered to be treatable with injected insulin by Banting and Best (1921, Nobel 1923) — life expectancy of Type 1 patients went from months to decades within a year of insulin's availability.

Type 2 diabetes: insulin RESISTANCE develops in target tissues. Beta cells initially compensate (more insulin) then eventually fail. Affects ~10% of adults globally. Strongly linked to obesity and inactivity.

The brain is unique in burning glucose nearly exclusively (~120 g/day, 20% of total body glucose use) — which is why hypoglycaemia causes confusion, seizures and unconsciousness within minutes.
items.why: Hormones feel like signals from somewhere distant. In glucose regulation, two opposing hormones from the same gland keep blood sugar within a tight band — a textbook example of antagonistic negative feedback.

items.title: Plants can push water up — but only a few metres
items.claim: Roots actively pump ions into the xylem at night. Water follows by osmosis, generating pressure that pushes sap upward. You can see it as guttation: droplets of liquid forced out at leaf tips in the morning.
items.prompt: Why does root pressure not lift water all the way to a redwood canopy?

options.text: Roots don't generate any pressure
Root pressure rarely exceeds ~0.2 MPa — enough to push water ~20 metres. Taller transport requires transpiration-driven tension at the leaves (cohesion-tension theory)
Root pressure works only horizontally
Water cannot move upward in plants

items.reveal:
Two mechanisms drive xylem flow:

1. Root pressure (positive): active ion transport into xylem; water follows; positive pressure pushes sap upward. Works in small herbaceous plants, in young growing tissue, and in trees in early spring before leaves open. Maxes out at ~0.2 MPa.

2. Transpiration pull (tension, cohesion-tension theory): evaporation at leaves creates negative pressure; cohesive water column transmits the pull down to roots. Routinely reaches -1 to -2 MPa. Works in any tree height up to ~130 m.

Guttation is visible evidence of root pressure: drops of xylem sap forced out of hydathodes on leaf tips overnight (when stomata are closed and transpiration cannot relieve the pressure). Looks like dew but contains dissolved minerals.

Most mature trees rely entirely on transpiration pull. Root pressure becomes detectable only when transpiration is suppressed (humid nights, plant chopped down, etc.).

Notably, mosses lack vascular tissue entirely and rely on diffusion and capillary action — which is why they top out at ~20 cm.
items.why: Roots seem like obvious pumps. They are — but only weak ones. The real heavy lifting in tall plants is done by evaporation at the top, pulling on water held together by hydrogen bonds.

items.title: Sugar in plants flows from wherever it's made to wherever it's needed
items.claim: Xylem carries water in one direction: up. Phloem carries dissolved sugars in any direction — up, down, lateral — from 'sources' (leaves, storage organs being mobilised) to 'sinks' (roots, fruits, growing tips). The same phloem tube can reverse direction with the season.
items.prompt: What drives bidirectional sugar transport?

options.text: Active pumps in every cell

Pressure-flow (Munch) hypothesis: sugar loaded at the source raises osmotic pressure there, drawing in water from xylem; unloaded sugar at the sink reduces pressure; bulk flow proceeds from high to low pressure along the phloem
Capillary action
Diffusion alone

items.reveal:
Phloem sieve tubes are living cells (unlike xylem vessels, which are dead). Companion cells help load sugar into sieve elements at sources.
