Loading: at a source (e.g., a photosynthesising leaf), sucrose is actively pumped INTO sieve elements via H+/sucrose symporters. Sucrose concentration rises to 1 mol/L. Water enters by osmosis. Hydrostatic pressure builds.

Unloading: at a sink (a fruit, root, or growing meristem), sucrose is removed and metabolised or stored. Water exits. Pressure drops.

The pressure gradient pushes sap from source to sink at ~1 metre/hour — much slower than xylem flow but still bulk flow.

Direction reverses seasonally. In spring, a deciduous tree's stored root sugars are sources, mobilising to buds (sinks). In summer, leaves are sources, fruits and roots are sinks. In autumn, leaves dump sugars to storage organs before falling.

Aphids tap phloem with their stylets and benefit from the natural pressure — sap is forced out of them as honeydew. Scientists use severed aphid stylets as natural phloem sampling needles.
items.why: Plant transport feels static. The phloem is a dynamic, switchable distribution network with pressure-driven bulk flow — and it can reverse direction within a single growing season.

items.title: Plants bend toward light by growing more on the dark side
items.claim: A potted plant on a windowsill tilts toward the window within hours. It doesn't push or twist — it grows ASYMMETRICALLY. Cells on the shaded side elongate faster than cells on the lit side, bending the stem toward the light.
items.prompt: What drives the asymmetric growth?

options.text: Mechanical tension from gravity

Auxin (indole-3-acetic acid) accumulates on the shaded side and stimulates cell elongation; this differential auxin distribution was demonstrated by Frits Went and Charles Darwin in classic shoot-tip experiments
Water collects on the dark side
Light evaporates cells on the lit side

items.reveal_title: Darwin's coleoptiles to Went's agar blocks
items.reveal:
Charles Darwin (1880, 'The Power of Movement in Plants', with son Francis) showed that the tip of a grass coleoptile senses light, but the bending occurs lower down — implying a signal travels.

Boysen-Jensen (1913) showed a thin agar block between the tip and the bending region allows the signal through; mica does not. The signal is chemical.

Frits Went (1928) collected the signal in agar blocks and applied it asymmetrically to decapitated coleoptiles, causing bending. The substance was named auxin (Greek auxein, 'to grow').

Mechanism: blue light receptors (phototropins) on the lit side trigger redistribution of PIN auxin efflux carriers. Auxin pumps preferentially to the shaded side. Higher auxin there causes cell wall loosening (expansin proteins) and elongation. The stem bends.

Auxin's reach extends beyond phototropism: apical dominance (shoot tip suppresses lateral buds), root gravitropism (concentrations bend roots DOWN), fruit development, leaf abscission, callus formation in tissue culture. It's the master plant hormone.
items.why: Plant movement seems passive. Phototropism is an active, hormonal, asymmetric growth response — controlled by a single small molecule with effects across the whole plant's life cycle.

items.title: Mosses spend most of their lives haploid — like permanent eggs
items.claim: Animals are diploid (two copies of each chromosome) and reduce to haploid (one copy) only briefly in sperm and eggs. Mosses live mostly as haploid (gametophyte) plants. The diploid sporophyte is a tiny stalk that grows from the haploid plant, makes spores, and dies.
items.prompt: What does alternation of generations mean?

options.text: Plants alternate between adult and juvenile forms

The life cycle alternates between a multicellular haploid stage (gametophyte) and a multicellular diploid stage (sporophyte); both are 'organisms' in their own right, unlike animals where only the diploid stage is recognisable as an individual
Genes alternate between being expressed and silent
Generations alternate between male and female

items.reveal:
The full plant life cycle: gametes (haploid, n) fuse to make a zygote (diploid, 2n) -> sporophyte (2n) develops -> meiosis -> spores (n) -> spores germinate into gametophytes (n) -> gametophytes make gametes (n) -> cycle repeats.

Mosses: gametophyte dominant (the leafy green plant). Sporophyte is the stalk with a capsule, attached to and dependent on the gametophyte.

Ferns: sporophyte dominant (the leafy plant). Gametophyte is a tiny independent heart-shaped prothallus, easy to miss.

Flowering plants: sporophyte hugely dominant (the tree, the grass). Gametophyte is microscopic — pollen grains (male, 3 cells) and embryo sacs inside ovules (female, 7-8 cells). Both are dependent on the sporophyte parent.

Evolutionary trend: gametophytes have become progressively smaller, more dependent, more protected. Flowering plants reduce them to barely-cellular structures.

In animals, only the diploid stage is multicellular; gametes are single cells. No alternation in the plant sense.
items.why: The 'plant' you see in your garden is one of two organisms in a single life cycle. The other organism — the gametophyte — has been reduced and hidden in flowering plants, but it's still there inside every pollen grain.

items.title: A 32,000-year-old seed grew into a flower
items.claim: In 2012, Russian scientists germinated seeds from a Silene stenophylla plant buried in Siberian permafrost about 32,000 years ago. Even outside such extremes, soil under most fields holds millions of viable seeds per hectare — a 'seed bank' waiting for the right conditions.
items.prompt: How can seeds survive so long?

options.text: They keep growing slowly

Dehydrated seeds enter a state of suspended metabolism (similar to tardigrades): low water content, vitrified protective sugars (raffinose, sucrose), late-embryogenesis-abundant (LEA) proteins, and physical/chemical dormancy mechanisms that block germination until cues like fire, scarification or freeze-thaw are met
Seeds photosynthesise underground
They eat surrounding soil microbes

items.reveal:
Seeds drop into soil constantly. Most germinate or die within a year. Some develop dormancy — physical (hard coat blocks water entry until scratched), physiological (chemical inhibitors must be degraded), or morphological (embryo must mature further).

A typical arable field has ~20-50 million weed seeds per hectare in the top 25 cm of soil. Many remain viable for 10-100 years. A few species (Verbascum, Chenopodium) have been germinated from soil samples 60+ years old.

The Silene seeds were buried by ice age squirrels in their burrows. Russian scientists grew tissue from the placenta of the immature fruits and regenerated the plants — not strictly seeds, but the same physiology.

Oldest unequivocally germinated seed: 2000-year-old date palm from Masada (Israel), germinated 2005.

The Svalbard Global Seed Vault (2008) stores ~1 million seed accessions at -18 C to preserve global crop diversity. The principle is the same as natural seed banks: dehydration plus cold preserves embryos near-indefinitely.

Disturbing a forest soil triggers mass germination as buried weed seeds suddenly see light. The 'memory' of the soil shapes what grows after disturbance.
items.why: Seeds look inert. Inside is a paused embryo, sometimes thousands of years on hold, waiting for the chemistry of damp soil and warmth to resume the life it interrupted.

items.title: Plants tell the date by measuring the LENGTH of the night
items.claim: Chrysanthemums flower in autumn. Spinach bolts in long-day summer. Plants 'know' the time of year. They don't measure day length — they measure how long the night is, by counting protein degradation events.
items.prompt: What molecules let plants measure night length?

options.text: An internal calendar

Phytochromes — light-absorbing pigments that switch between two forms (Pr and Pfr); the ratio shifts in the dark by slow Pfr decay, and the time taken to reach a threshold tells the plant how long the night was
Temperature alone
Magnetic field sensing

items.reveal:
Phytochrome exists in two interconverting forms: Pr (red-absorbing) and Pfr (far-red-absorbing). Red light (660 nm) converts Pr to Pfr; far-red light (730 nm) reverses it. In darkness, Pfr slowly degrades back to Pr.

Day-length detection works on NIGHT length. Interrupting a long night with a brief flash of red light is enough to convert Pr to Pfr and 'reset' the plant — and shows that the plant is timing darkness, not light. Far-red light reverses the effect (Borthwick, Hendricks 1950s).

Short-day plants (chrysanthemums, soybeans, rice) flower when nights exceed a critical length. Long-day plants (spinach, wheat, lettuce) flower when nights are shorter than a critical length. Day-neutral plants (tomatoes, sunflowers) flower at a certain age.

The signal travels from leaves to apical meristem. The mobile signal — long sought as 'florigen' (Chailakhyan 1937) — was finally identified in 2007 as the FT protein (FLOWERING LOCUS T).

Agricultural exploitation: greenhouses can artificially adjust day length to force flowering year-round. Cut-flower industries rely on photoperiod manipulation.
items.why: Plants seem time-blind. They use a beautiful molecular clock built from light-reversible pigments — and they care about the dark, not the light.

items.title: Light makes the inside of a chloroplast 1000 times more acidic
items.claim: In dark chloroplasts, stroma and thylakoid lumen are both about pH 7. Turn on the light: protons are pumped from stroma INTO thylakoid lumen. Lumen pH drops to ~5; stroma rises to ~8. That's a thousand-fold proton concentration difference.
items.prompt: What's the point?

options.text: Acidic conditions help photosynthesis

The proton gradient drives ATP synthase: protons flow back through the enzyme from lumen to stroma, powering ATP synthesis. The light reactions store light energy as a transmembrane proton gradient, just as respiration does
Low pH activates chlorophyll
Acidic environment kills competing bacteria

items.reveal:
Light reactions in chloroplast thylakoid membranes:
1. Photosystem II uses light to oxidise water (releasing O2) and reduce plastoquinone. Protons are released INSIDE the lumen.
2. Cytochrome b6f passes electrons on while also pumping protons FROM stroma TO lumen.
3. Photosystem I uses light to push electrons to NADP+, making NADPH (in the stroma).
4. Net result: lumen accumulates protons, stroma loses them. pH gradient ~3 units (1000x concentration).

ATP synthase (CF1-CF0) in the thylakoid membrane lets protons flow back from lumen to stroma. The enzyme rotates, synthesises ATP from ADP and Pi. ATP and NADPH are released INTO the stroma, where the Calvin cycle uses them to fix CO2.

This is exactly analogous to mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation. Same chemistry, opposite source — solar input rather than food oxidation. Both use the proton motive force to make ATP.

The parallel was predicted by Peter Mitchell in 1961 and confirmed experimentally over the next two decades.
items.why: Photosynthesis is taught as if it makes sugar directly from light. Light first powers a proton pump; the pump powers ATP synthesis; ATP plus NADPH then power sugar synthesis. Energy storage is layered.

items.title: Plants and oceans cycle far more CO2 than humans release — yet we still drive the trend
items.claim: Humans emit ~10 gigatonnes of carbon per year. Natural fluxes (photosynthesis ~120 Gt, ocean exchange ~80 Gt, respiration ~120 Gt) dwarf this. Yet atmospheric CO2 keeps rising. The natural fluxes are roughly balanced — human emissions are a small but unmatched addition.
items.prompt: Why does a small flux dominate the trend?

options.text: Human CO2 is chemically different

The large natural fluxes are bidirectional and roughly balanced; the small human flux is NET addition. Imagine a bath whose inflow exactly equals outflow — a slow added trickle raises the water level whether the main flow is large or not
Plants absorb only certain types of CO2
Ocean has stopped absorbing CO2

items.reveal_title: Flux vs reservoir vs net change
items.reveal:
Reservoirs (rough sizes in gigatonnes of carbon):
Atmosphere: ~880 (and rising)
Oceans: ~38,000 (most as dissolved bicarbonate, slow exchange with deep ocean)
Soils: ~1,500-2,400
Vegetation: ~450-650
Fossil fuels: ~4,000+ (decreasing as we burn them)

Fluxes (Gt C per year):
Photosynthesis: ~120 (atmosphere to land)
Land respiration: ~120 (back to atmosphere)
Ocean uptake: ~80 (atmosphere to ocean)
Ocean release: ~78 (ocean to atmosphere)
Fossil emissions: ~10 (geological store to atmosphere)
Land-use change: ~1-2 net (mostly deforestation)

The natural fluxes are within ~1% of balance. The fossil flux is unbalanced — it's NET addition with no matching natural removal at the same scale. About half is absorbed by oceans and land 'sinks'; half stays airborne. Atmospheric CO2 rises ~2.5 ppm/year.

Residence time vs adjustment time: an individual CO2 molecule exchanges with the ocean in years. But removing the EXCESS takes much longer (hundreds to thousands of years for the surface ocean, ~100,000 years for full geological recovery).
items.why: The 'humans only emit 4% of CO2 turnover' argument confuses flux with net change. A small net addition into a near-balanced cycle is what matters, and it accumulates.

items.title: Bread, beer and yoghurt all use the same biochemical loophole
items.claim: Without oxygen, glycolysis stops because cells run out of NAD+. Yeasts solve this by reducing pyruvate to ethanol (and releasing CO2). Muscles and lactic acid bacteria solve it by reducing pyruvate to lactate. Different products, same problem.
items.prompt: What's the shared logic?

options.text: Both make ATP from the products
Both regenerate NAD+ from NADH so glycolysis can continue producing ATP (2 per glucose); the pyruvate must be 'dealt with' chemically because no oxygen is available to oxidise it via the Krebs cycle
Both produce oxygen
Both ferment only certain sugars

items.reveal_title: NAD+ regeneration as the key step
items.reveal:
Glycolysis converts glucose to 2 pyruvate, producing 2 ATP and 2 NADH (reduced electron carrier). For glycolysis to continue running, NAD+ must be regenerated.

Aerobic cells: pyruvate enters mitochondria; Krebs cycle and electron transport oxidise NADH back to NAD+; oxygen is the final electron acceptor.

Anaerobic conditions: no oxygen, so no electron transport. Cells use pyruvate as the electron acceptor instead, dumping electrons from NADH onto it.

Yeasts (alcoholic fermentation): pyruvate -> acetaldehyde (releasing CO2) -> ethanol (using NADH, regenerating NAD+). Result: 2 ATP per glucose, plus ethanol and CO2. Bread rises from the CO2; beer accumulates ethanol.

Muscle and lactic acid bacteria (lactic fermentation): pyruvate -> lactate (using NADH, regenerating NAD+). Result: 2 ATP per glucose, plus lactic acid. Soured milk -> yoghurt; cabbage -> sauerkraut.

Aerobic respiration is about 15x more efficient (30-32 ATP vs 2). Fermentation is faster and works without oxygen. Both have their place.

Some organisms (facultative anaerobes like E. coli) switch between the two. Strict aerobes (most animals) die without oxygen within minutes. Strict anaerobes (Clostridium) die WITH oxygen — for them, O2 is toxic.
items.why: Bread, beer, wine, yoghurt and sauerkraut all rely on the same chemical trick to regenerate NAD+. Human civilisation has built food traditions on top of microbial anaerobic biochemistry.

items.title: Birds breathe in a circle — air flows one way through their lungs
items.claim: Mammal lungs are tidal: air goes in, then back out the same way. Bird lungs are unidirectional: air flows through the gas-exchange surfaces in one direction continuously, fed by air sacs that act as bellows. This is why bar-headed geese can cross the Himalayas at 9000 metres.
items.prompt: What's the advantage of unidirectional flow?

options.text: Allows louder vocalisations
Gas exchange surfaces are constantly washed with fresh, high-oxygen air rather than a mix of fresh and 'used' air; this allows higher O2 extraction efficiency, critical for flight at altitude
Birds need less oxygen than mammals
It cools them down faster

items.reveal:
Birds have rigid lungs and ~9 flexible air sacs distributed through the body. The sacs act as bellows; the lungs are where exchange happens.

Two respiratory cycles move one breath through:
First inhalation: air goes to posterior air sacs.
First exhalation: air flows from posterior sacs through the parabronchi (gas exchange surfaces) toward the anterior sacs.
Second inhalation: air moves to anterior sacs.
Second exhalation: air leaves the body.

The parabronchi see fresh-O2 air on both inhalation AND exhalation, in the same direction. No 'dead space' mixing.

Advantages: at altitude where O2 partial pressure is low (Mount Everest summit is ~30% sea level), bird lungs maintain steeper gradients for gas exchange. Bar-headed geese routinely cross the Himalayas at 6000-7000 metres, occasionally higher.

Mammals top out around 6000 m without acclimatisation; even Sherpa adaptations don't match bird physiology.

The unidirectional system may have evolved from theropod dinosaurs. Fossil evidence suggests the bone pneumatisation (hollow bones, air sacs) appeared before flight.
items.why: Lungs are usually imagined as bellows you fill and empty. Birds' fundamentally different design — air sacs as bellows and lungs as flow-through gas exchangers — outperforms mammals at altitude and is one of vertebrate biology's underappreciated marvels.

items.title: You convert nitrogen waste into your own pee chemistry every day
items.claim: Breaking down amino acids releases ammonia (NH3) — toxic to cells at concentrations above ~50 micromolar. Mammals convert it to urea, a relatively harmless molecule that can be safely concentrated and excreted in urine. Fish dump ammonia directly into water; birds convert it to uric acid.
items.prompt: Why do different animals handle nitrogen waste differently?

options.text: Random evolutionary chance

Water availability drives the choice: fish (ammoniotelic, ammonia) need lots of water for dilution; mammals (ureotelic, urea) use moderate water; birds and reptiles (uricotelic, uric acid) save water by making a near-solid waste — important for desert and egg-laying animals
Different chemistries fit different diets
All animals make urea

items.reveal:
Ammonia (NH3): produced by deamination of amino acids. Toxic at low concentrations. Fish, most aquatic invertebrates excrete it directly through gills — the surrounding water dilutes it.

Urea: synthesised by the urea cycle in the liver (Krebs and Henseleit, 1932 — the same Hans Krebs who later won the Nobel for the citric acid cycle). Five reactions, costs 4 ATP per urea. Each urea carries 2 nitrogen atoms. Soluble, moderately concentrated in urine (up to ~50x blood concentration in humans).

Uric acid: birds, reptiles, insects. Synthesis costs even more energy than urea (~10 ATP per nitrogen handled) but precipitates as semi-solid pellets, requiring almost no water for excretion. The white component of bird droppings is uric acid.

Note: egg-laying animals (birds, reptiles, monotremes) need a non-toxic, water-poor waste form that won't poison the developing embryo. Uric acid fits the niche.

In humans, uric acid is a byproduct of nucleic acid breakdown (not protein). Gout is precipitation of uric acid crystals in joints.

Marine mammals (whales, seals) face the opposite challenge: no fresh water for dilution. They use highly concentrated urine instead.
items.why: Waste seems like a non-design decision. The form of nitrogen excretion is one of evolution's deepest trade-offs — tying physiology, water economy and even reproductive biology together.

items.title: Remove three quarters of a liver and it grows back
items.claim: Humans can lose 70-75% of their liver (in surgery or donation) and regrow it to original size within weeks. The liver is the only solid human organ with this level of regenerative ability. Even other strongly regenerative tissues (skin, bone marrow) can't grow back this much organ.
items.prompt: How does it regenerate?

options.text: A reservoir of liver stem cells expands

Mature hepatocytes (normally quiescent) re-enter the cell cycle and divide; growth factors (HGF, EGF, IL-6) signal the remaining cells to proliferate until the original organ mass is restored, then stop
Surrounding organs grow into the missing space
The bile duct generates new liver tissue

items.reveal:
Normal adult liver: hepatocytes (~80% of liver cells) sit in G0, dividing at most once every year or two. Cellular workhorses doing biochemistry, not growing.

After partial hepatectomy (surgical removal): within hours, growth factors (hepatocyte growth factor HGF, EGF, TGF-alpha) surge in the portal blood. Hepatocytes enter S phase by 24-48 hours, divide, and continue dividing until liver mass returns. Then they switch off and resume their quiescent state.

Full regeneration in 2-3 weeks. Donors who give part of their liver for transplant recover their original liver mass and function.

Limit: the regeneration requires intact liver remnant. Cirrhotic livers — where hepatocytes have been replaced by scar tissue — cannot regenerate. Acute liver failure with widespread cell death may also overwhelm the regenerative response.

The Prometheus myth (vulture eats his liver, which regrows nightly) suggests ancient Greek anatomists may have noticed liver regeneration. Modern molecular understanding mostly dates from the 1980s-90s.

The liver's regenerative capacity is one of the foundations of living donor transplants — a partial donation to a recipient leaves both with functional livers.
items.why: Major organ regrowth seems out of reach for mammals. The liver does it routinely — and the molecular signals are now well enough understood to be co-opted for transplant medicine.

items.title: Your entire skeleton is rebuilt every 10 years
items.claim: Bone seems inert. It isn't. Osteoclasts dissolve bone; osteoblasts lay down new bone. The balance maintains structure but constantly turns over the material. In adults, about 10% of bone is replaced each year.
items.prompt: Why turn over a structural tissue at all?

options.text: Bone cannot heal otherwise
Continuous remodelling repairs microdamage (fatigue cracks from daily loading), regulates calcium and phosphate balance, and lets bone adapt to changing mechanical demands (Wolff's law)
Bone serves no structural purpose
Hormones require fresh bone

items.reveal_title: Wolff's law and the calcium reservoir
items.reveal:
Three cell types in bone:
- Osteoblasts: deposit new bone matrix (collagen + hydroxyapatite mineral).
- Osteocytes: mature former osteoblasts embedded in bone matrix; sense mechanical loads.
- Osteoclasts: multinucleate cells that dissolve bone (acid + proteases).

Normal turnover: ~10% of skeleton per year in adults. Trabecular (cancellous) bone turns over faster than cortical bone. Whole-skeleton replacement takes 7-10 years.

Wolff's law (Julius Wolff, 1892): bone adapts to load. Loaded bone strengthens; unloaded bone weakens. Astronauts lose ~1-2% of bone mass per month in microgravity. Bedridden patients similarly. Athletes have denser bones in heavily-used regions (dominant arm of tennis players).

Calcium balance: 99% of body calcium is in bones. The blood calcium pool is small (~10 mmol total) but vital (cardiac function, nerve signalling). Parathyroid hormone mobilises calcium from bone when blood calcium drops; calcitonin reduces calcium release when it rises. Bone is a buffer.

Osteoporosis: net imbalance favouring resorption, especially post-menopause (oestrogen normally restrains osteoclasts). Hip and vertebral fractures rise dramatically.
items.why: Bone looks like stone. Functionally it's a dynamic tissue with continuous renewal, mechanical adaptation, and calcium economy — none of which is visible from the outside but all of which keeps the skeleton viable.

items.title: A mouse uses more energy per gram than an elephant
items.claim: Kleiber's law: metabolic rate scales as body mass to the 3/4 power. Bigger animals have lower metabolic rate per unit mass. A mouse uses ~50x more calories per gram per day than an elephant.
items.prompt: Why scaling exponent of 3/4 and not 1 or 2/3?

options.text: It's a measurement coincidence

Surface-area scaling (2/3) would predict heat loss only. The 3/4 exponent reflects the geometry of branching vascular and respiratory networks delivering resources to cells (West, Brown, Enquist 1997)
Because heart rate scales as mass
All animals have the same metabolic rate

items.reveal:
Max Kleiber (1932): metabolic rate (B) scales as body mass (M) to the 3/4. B = a * M^0.75. Holds from mice to elephants over six orders of magnitude.

Consequences:
- Mass-specific rate (B/M) scales as M^(-1/4). A 30 gram mouse uses ~50x more O2 per gram than a 3000 kg elephant.
- Heart rate scales as M^(-1/4). Mice: ~600 bpm; humans: ~70 bpm; elephants: ~30 bpm; blue whales: ~10 bpm.
- Lifespan scales as M^(1/4). Mice live 2-3 years; humans 80; whales 100+.
- Total heartbeats per lifetime are roughly constant (~1-2 billion) across mammals (with humans as an outlier — we get more).

The 3/4 exponent puzzled biologists for decades. West, Brown and Enquist (1997, Science) proposed it falls out of optimal branching transport networks (vascular trees, lungs). The model fits remarkably well across taxa.

Applications: drug dosing across species (allometric scaling guides initial doses); ecological energetics (predicting how many predators a habitat can support); aging research (the 'rate of living' hypothesis links metabolism to lifespan).
items.why: Per-gram metabolic rate is highly NOT constant across animals. Body size determines life pace — fast or slow — through physical constraints on how internal transport networks scale.

items.title: Your brain is rinsed clean of waste only when you sleep
items.claim: The brain has no lymphatic vessels for waste removal. Instead, during sleep, cerebrospinal fluid flows through brain tissue via the glymphatic system, washing out metabolic waste including amyloid-beta (linked to Alzheimer's). The pathway is 60% more open during sleep than waking.
items.prompt: What changes between sleep and wake?

options.text: Blood flow doubles

During sleep, brain interstitial space expands (~60%), allowing CSF to flow rapidly through it; during waking, the space is smaller and flow is reduced. Cellular debris and protein aggregates clear faster while you sleep
The brain stops producing waste
Waste is excreted through the eyes

items.reveal:
Maiken Nedergaard's lab (Xie et al., Science 2013) discovered that the brain's waste-clearance pathway is dramatically more active during sleep.

Mechanism: cerebrospinal fluid enters the brain along arterial perivascular spaces, mixes with interstitial fluid, and exits along venous perivascular spaces, carrying waste with it. Aquaporin-4 channels on astrocyte endfeet are critical.

During sleep, brain cells shrink (~60% increase in interstitial volume), allowing much faster bulk flow. The amount of amyloid-beta (a protein implicated in Alzheimer's) cleared during sleep is roughly double that of waking.

Mice with disrupted glymphatic flow accumulate amyloid-beta and develop cognitive decline. Chronic poor sleep is increasingly linked epidemiologically to Alzheimer's risk in humans.

This is one of the strongest known reasons for sleep — and was discovered only in 2013. Sleep had been one of biology's biggest unsolved 'why' questions.

Other sleep functions: memory consolidation (especially REM), synaptic homeostasis (downscaling synapse strength to make room for new learning), immune function. The brain seems to use sleep for many heavy housekeeping operations.
items.why: Sleep was a mystery for decades. One major answer turns out to be: the brain literally rinses itself. Skipping sleep means accumulating molecular debris.

items.title: Lizards aren't cold-blooded — they outsource thermoregulation
items.claim: Reptiles are usually called 'cold-blooded'. They aren't — many maintain body temperatures within 1-2 C of their preferred range. They do it behaviourally: basking on rocks, retreating to shade, postural adjustments — instead of metabolically.
items.prompt: What does 'ectotherm' actually mean?

options.text: Cold internal body temperature
Body temperature regulated primarily by external heat sources (sun, surfaces) rather than internal metabolic heat production; the animal's behaviour does the thermoregulation
Inability to thermoregulate at all
Low blood temperature

items.reveal:
Endotherm vs ectotherm is about the SOURCE of body heat, not the temperature itself:
- Endotherm: internal heat from metabolism. Mammals and birds. Maintains body temperature by burning calories continuously.
- Ectotherm: external heat from environment. Reptiles, amphibians, fish, invertebrates. Maintains body temperature by movement and posture.

A desert lizard might bask flattened against a north-facing rock at dawn (warming up), move to shade at midday (cooling off), retreat into a burrow at night. Body temperature can be held within 1-2 C of an ideal value (~35-37 C for many lizards) — surprisingly mammal-like, achieved completely without metabolic heat.

Advantages of being ectotherm: much lower energy requirements. A reptile can survive on ~10% of the food a mammal of equivalent size needs. Snakes can fast for months.

Disadvantages: limited cold tolerance, dependent on environmental cues, slow at low temperatures. Reptiles cannot live in deep polar regions.

Many 'cold-blooded' fish, like tuna, are partially endothermic in muscle and brain (regional endothermy). And some plants (Symplocarpus, skunk cabbage) generate metabolic heat to melt snow and attract pollinators — endothermic plants exist.
items.why: 'Cold-blooded' is a misleading term. Reptiles regulate body temperature carefully — they just do it with behaviour and the sun, not with the calories you'd otherwise burn.

items.title: Your muscles cannot share their sugar reserves with your brain
items.claim: Your body stores carbohydrate as glycogen. The liver holds ~100 grams; skeletal muscle ~400 grams. The liver's glycogen feeds the blood and brain. Muscle glycogen is for muscle's own use — it cannot release glucose to the bloodstream.
items.prompt: Why can the liver release glucose to blood but muscle cannot?

options.text: Muscle is too far from blood vessels

Liver expresses glucose-6-phosphatase, the enzyme that removes the phosphate from glucose-6-phosphate so glucose can leave the cell; skeletal muscle does not have this enzyme, so the breakdown product is trapped and used locally
Muscle glycogen is chemically different
Blood vessels don't enter muscle

items.reveal:
Glycogen breakdown:
1. Glycogen phosphorylase clips glucose-1-phosphate off the glycogen chain.
2. Phosphoglucomutase converts it to glucose-6-phosphate.
3. To leave the cell, the phosphate must be removed (glucose can cross membranes, but glucose-6-phosphate cannot).

Liver and kidney have glucose-6-phosphatase — they CAN remove the phosphate and export free glucose into the blood, supplying the brain and red blood cells.

Muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase. The glucose-6-phosphate must be used locally — typically immediately entering glycolysis for ATP production.

The Cori cycle compensates indirectly: muscle generates lactate (during anaerobic exertion), exports it to the liver, where it's converted back to glucose (gluconeogenesis) and shipped back to muscle.

Von Gierke's disease (glycogen storage disease type I) is an inherited deficiency of glucose-6-phosphatase: even liver glycogen cannot be exported. Patients have severe fasting hypoglycaemia.

Liver glycogen depletes in ~24 hours of fasting; muscle glycogen depletes in ~90 minutes of hard exercise. After that, fat and (eventually) protein become the energy source.
items.why: Sugar storage feels like a shared pool. It isn't — the body has specialised tissue-level energy compartments, controlled by which enzymes each tissue expresses.

items.title: Jellyfish swim and hunt with no brain
items.claim: A jellyfish has no central nervous system. Just a 'nerve net' distributed across its body. Yet it swims rhythmically, captures prey, navigates currents, and (in some species) processes visual information from 24 separate eyes.
items.prompt: How does a decentralised nervous system coordinate behaviour?

options.text: It doesn't really — jellyfish drift passively

Nerve nets are distributed neural networks where any neuron can communicate with neighbours in all directions; rhythmic pacemakers (rhopalia in many medusae) generate swimming signals that propagate across the bell
Each cell acts independently
Jellyfish have a hidden tiny brain

items.reveal:
Cnidarians (jellyfish, corals, sea anemones, Hydra) are among the simplest animals with nervous systems. They have a nerve NET rather than centralised ganglia or a brain.

Nerves form a diffuse 2D network across the body wall. Many cnidarian neurons are 'bipolar' — propagating signals in either direction. The network has no obvious centre. Synapses are often non-polarised.

Despite the apparent simplicity, cnidarians produce coordinated behaviour:
- Rhythmic bell pulsations for swimming (governed by 'rhopalia' — small sensory clusters around the bell margin in most jellyfish).
- Coordinated tentacle action for prey capture.
- Light avoidance (Hydra), vertical migration (many planktonic jellyfish).
- Box jellyfish (Cubozoa) have 24 eyes in 4 'rhopalia' — including image-forming lensed eyes that probably do visual navigation around mangrove obstacles, despite no centralised processor.

The nerve net is evolutionarily ancestral. As bilaterians (most other animals) developed bilateral symmetry, they evolved centralised nervous systems (brains and ventral or dorsal nerve cords). Cnidarians stayed with the decentralised model and still do well.

Decentralised processing has appeared independently in some bilaterian groups too — echinoderms (starfish, sea urchins) have radial nerve cords without a brain.
items.why: Brains feel essential to animal behaviour. Jellyfish show how much can be done without one — distributed processing, rhythmic generators and sensory clusters can produce sophisticated behaviour.

items.title: About 90% of your serotonin is made in your gut
items.claim: Serotonin is famous as a mood-related brain chemical. But ~90% of the body's serotonin is in the gut, where it regulates gut motility and is influenced by gut bacteria. The gut and brain communicate via the vagus nerve and circulating molecules.
items.prompt: What's the gut-brain axis?

options.text: A direct neural connection like an optic nerve

A multi-channel system: vagus nerve sends ~80% afferent (gut-to-brain) signals; immune signalling; circulating short-chain fatty acids and neurotransmitters from gut bacteria — all influence brain function bidirectionally
An indirect blood-flow link only
A myth — the gut and brain don't talk

items.reveal_title: The enteric nervous system and microbial signals
items.reveal:
The gut has its own nervous system (the enteric nervous system, ENS) with ~500 million neurons — about as many as a cat's brain. The ENS controls gut motility, secretion and absorption largely independently of the central nervous system.

The vagus nerve connects gut and brain. About 80% of vagus fibres are afferent (carrying signals FROM gut TO brain). Gut chemical and stretch receptors continuously inform the brain about digestive state.

Serotonin: ~90% is in enterochromaffin cells of the gut, regulating peristalsis and pain signalling. Drugs targeting gut serotonin (e.g., 5-HT3 antagonists) treat IBS and chemotherapy nausea.

Gut bacteria contribute by:
- Producing short-chain fatty acids (butyrate, propionate) from fibre, which affect blood-brain barrier permeability and microglial function.
- Producing or modulating neurotransmitters (GABA, serotonin precursors).
- Influencing tryptophan metabolism (the precursor for serotonin).
- Modulating systemic inflammation.

Germ-free mice (raised without bacteria) show altered behaviour, anxiety, and brain development — restored by giving them normal gut bacteria. Effects in humans are more modest but real (e.g., faecal microbiota transplants can influence mood markers in some patients).

The gut-brain field is young and much remains speculative. Causal direction and effect sizes in humans are still being mapped.
items.why: Brain chemistry feels like brain-only territory. Much of our serotonin is in the gut; bacteria influence brain function via multiple routes. The body's signalling architecture is broader than its anatomy suggests.

items.title: The avocado was made for a giant ground sloth
items.claim: Avocado fruit has a huge stone surrounded by lipid-rich flesh. No living mammal can swallow it whole. The fruit's design anticipated a disperser — likely the now-extinct Pleistocene megafauna (giant ground sloths, gomphotheres). The plant outlived its partner.
items.prompt: What does this tell us about coevolution?

options.text: Coevolution always succeeds

Plants and dispersers shape each other's traits over millions of years; when the partner goes extinct, the plant may persist with traits that look maladaptive in the present — ecological 'ghosts of evolution past'
Plants don't need animals for dispersal
Coevolved plants always go extinct with their partners

items.reveal:
Daniel Janzen and Paul Martin (1982) proposed the concept of 'anachronistic fruits': fruits whose size, hardness, smell or chemistry seem designed for dispersers that no longer exist.

North American megafauna went extinct ~13,000 years ago (climate change plus human hunting): mastodons, giant ground sloths (up to 6 metres tall), gomphotheres, glyptodonts. Many large-fruited Central American trees — avocados, papayas, large legume pods — appear to have coevolved with these animals.

Without megafaunal dispersal, these trees rely on humans, water, or rare alternatives (jaguars eat avocados; tapirs swallow some seeds whole). Many would have declining ranges if not for human cultivation.

Osage orange (Maclura pomifera): grapefruit-sized fruits with little use to modern animals. Likely a mastodon plant. Now native to a small Texas range; spread widely only because humans use it as windbreaks and hedges.

Coffee, cacao, durian — all probably coevolved with mammalian dispersers and rely on living relatives or human cultivation for survival.

The broader point: present-day ecology contains relics from past ecologies. Some traits make sense only in the context of vanished species and lost interactions.
items.why: Coevolution implies tight mutual adaptation. When one partner disappears, the other can persist but appears strangely engineered for a world that no longer exists.

items.title: Wounded plants warn their neighbours via airborne chemicals
items.claim: An acacia tree being browsed by giraffes releases volatile chemicals (methyl jasmonate, ethylene). Downwind acacias detect the signal and produce defensive tannins within 30 minutes — before any herbivore has reached them.
items.prompt: Why warn other plants?

options.text: Pure altruism between trees

The signal probably evolved for systemic intra-plant communication (alerting other parts of the same tree); the inter-plant 'warning' is likely a by-product, though it does benefit kin or close neighbours under some conditions
Plants control each other's defences telepathically
It's a coincidence, not a signal

items.reveal_title: Volatile organic compounds in plant communication
items.reveal:
Wouter van Hoven (1980s) and Edward Farmer/Clarence Ryan (1990s) showed that plants under attack release volatile signals that other plants detect.

Mechanism: damaged tissue produces jasmonic acid; some is released as methyl jasmonate (volatile). Other plants take it in through stomata. It triggers expression of defensive genes — protease inhibitors that make leaves indigestible, tannins, alkaloids.

Other signals include green leaf volatiles (the smell of cut grass), terpenoids, ethylene. Each can trigger specific responses in receivers.

The original function is almost certainly within-plant: signalling from damaged leaves to undamaged ones via volatile leakage through the air, faster than through phloem in some cases. Lab tests show same-individual leaves respond as well as neighbours' leaves do.

Some plants also send volatile signals that attract predators of their herbivores. Maize plants attacked by caterpillars release blends specific to the caterpillar species, attracting parasitic wasps that lay eggs in the caterpillars.

'Crying plant' studies are controversial. Effect sizes vary by experiment, and the term 'warning' is anthropomorphic — but the chemistry is real, well-characterised, and has agricultural implications (push-pull pest management exploits these signals).
items.why: Plants seem passive. Volatile chemical signalling is widespread, sophisticated, and rich — and entire chemical 'languages' between plants and their herbivores and predators are still being decoded.

items.title: PCR exists because of a bacterium living in a hot spring
items.claim: Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) cycles between ~95 C (denature DNA) and ~60 C (anneal primers). Most enzymes would be cooked. PCR works because Taq polymerase, from Thermus aquaticus (Yellowstone hot springs), has a stable structure at boiling temperatures.
items.prompt: What's the significance?

options.text: Polymerase from any organism could work

Without a heat-stable polymerase, every PCR cycle would require fresh enzyme — impractical. Taq DNA polymerase survives 95 C and made automated PCR feasible (Mullis 1985, Nobel 1993), transforming molecular biology, forensics and medical diagnosis
Yellowstone bacteria are specially treated for use
PCR doesn't really need hot temperatures

items.reveal:
Thomas Brock isolated Thermus aquaticus from hot springs at Yellowstone in 1969, purely out of curiosity. He showed bacteria thrive at temperatures up to 80 C — far hotter than was thought possible at the time.

Fifteen years later, Kary Mullis (Cetus Corporation) invents PCR. The first version uses E. coli DNA polymerase — denatured each cycle, requiring fresh enzyme to be added every 30 seconds for 30+ cycles. Tedious.

Taq DNA polymerase, isolated from T. aquaticus, survives the high temperatures. PCR becomes automatable. The PCR machine — a programmable thermocycler — becomes a standard piece of every molecular lab.

PCR transformed:
- Molecular cloning (you can amplify any DNA without growing it in bacteria first).
- Genetic testing and diagnosis.
- Forensics (DNA fingerprinting from tiny samples).
- Genome sequencing (most methods start with PCR amplification).
- Real-time PCR for COVID-19 diagnosis during the pandemic.

Other extremophile biotech:
- Vent polymerases (from hydrothermal vents) for higher-fidelity PCR.
- Detergent enzymes (proteases, lipases) from psychrophilic bacteria work at low temperatures, allowing cold-water washing.
- DNA-melting and structure-determining enzymes from various thermophiles.

Basic research on 'irrelevant' bacteria led to a transformative technology.
items.why: PCR seems like an obvious technique. It required a bacterium that no one had a use for, found in a place no one expected life to be. Basic, curiosity-driven biology paid off enormously.

items.title: Trees in a forest can be physically connected to each other through fungi
items.claim: Most plant roots are colonised by mycorrhizal fungi. Filaments (hyphae) extend from one tree's root system through the soil to other trees, exchanging carbon, nutrients and chemical signals. The network has been called the 'wood wide web'.
items.prompt: What does the fungal network do?

options.text: Nothing — it's a fanciful idea

Mycorrhizal fungi exchange phosphorus and water for sugars with plant roots; the same fungal network often connects multiple trees, and there's evidence that carbon can flow from one tree to another along this network
Fungi feed only on dead plants
Trees connect to other trees directly without fungi

items.reveal:
About 80-90% of land plant species form mycorrhizal associations:
- Arbuscular mycorrhizae (AMF, Glomeromycota): hyphae penetrate root cells. Common in grasses, most flowering plants. Ancient (~400 million years, possibly enabled land plants to colonise dry land).
- Ectomycorrhizae (basidiomycetes and ascomycetes): hyphae form a sheath around roots and grow between cells. Common in temperate and boreal trees (pine, oak, birch).

The fungi gain sugars from the plant; the plant gains greatly expanded effective root surface area for nutrient and water absorption.

Networks: ectomycorrhizal fungi often colonise multiple trees with a continuous mycelium. Suzanne Simard's experiments (1997 Nature, follow-ups) used isotope-labelled carbon to show carbon flow between Douglas firs and paper birches via fungal connections.

The 'mother tree' hypothesis (Simard, popularised) is controversial — the magnitude and direction of carbon flow, and whether it represents 'communication' rather than diffusion, is still debated. Some recent reviews argue effects are smaller and less directional than originally claimed.

What's not in doubt: mycorrhizal networks are real, sometimes vast (one Armillaria fungus in Oregon covers 9.7 km^2 and is ~2400 years old), and important for nutrient cycling, drought tolerance and forest dynamics.

Agriculture is starting to take mycorrhizae seriously — many fertilizer regimes inadvertently suppress them, reducing long-term soil health.
items.why: Trees look like independent giants. Under the soil they are nodes in fungal networks — sharing nutrients, sometimes carbon, and almost certainly signals. The unit of life is harder to define than it looks.
